documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit mode collapse, where their output distribution concentrates on familiar semantic modes. When diversity disappears, repeated sampling becomes semantic repetition rather than discovery, making rare but stronger solutions unlikely to surface and leaving self-evolution and continual learning difficult to sustain. Most remedies intervene only at inference time, shaping sam- ples without making diversity a model capability. We propose PRISM, a training-time framework that internalizes diversity within the model. PRISM combines (i) submodular curation that pairs each prompt with diverse-yet-correct multi-teacher solutions, and (ii) stochastic embedding modulation, which turns special-token perturbations into implicit signals for sampling distinct outputs. A theoretical analysis establishes the stability of this mechanism. On WritingPrompts and BookMIA, PRISM moves the quality-diversity frontier outward, achieving the best generation quality in all model-benchmark settings while maintaining the strongest or near-strongest semantic diversity across two open-weight model families. It also improves sampling efficiency on math and code benchmarks. Beyond inference, PRISM yields a stronger foundation for reinforcement learning, sustaining diverse rollouts and mitigating the diversity collapse commonly observed during RL training.

NORA - The Norwegian Artificial Intelligence Research Consortium - works to strengthen Norwegian research, education and innovation within the fields of AI, machine learning and robotics. NORA is a collaboration between 9 universities, 4 university colleges and 4 research institutes. The current article provides a summary of NORA’s annual conference 2026.

This study documented the implementation and outcomes of Project HIRAYA (Honoring Industry Partners and Rewarding Accomplishment of Youth by Giving Awards), an innovative post-work immersion program at Cabarroguis National School of Arts and Trades, Quirino, Philippines. Grounded in experiential learning and formative assessment perspectives, the initiative aimed to recognize student accomplishments, strengthen school-industry partnerships, promote stakeholder engagement, and improve post-immersion evaluation. A descriptive innovation implementation and evaluation approach was employed using institutional records, student portfolios, performance assessment rubrics, oral interviews, monitoring reports, and stakeholder feedback. The project involved Grade 12 Senior High School students, work immersion teachers, school administrators, and industry partners. Student performance was assessed through industry partner evaluations (30%), teacher assessments (30%), oral interviews (30%), and portfolio evaluations (10%). Findings revealed an increase in participating industry partners from 41 to 55, formal recognition of industry contributions and outstanding student accomplishments, successful implementation of socialization activities and learning exhibits, and evaluation of 85% of student work immersion portfolios. However, delayed assessment submissions, scheduling conflicts, inconsistent exhibit documentation, and incomplete portfolios affected implementation efficiency. The study concluded that Project HIRAYA provided a structured mechanism for recognizing workplace learning achievements and reinforcing institutional collaboration. Institutionalization through the School Annual Implementation Plan, strengthened industry coordination, standardized assessment procedures, and development of a replication framework were recommended. The initiative aligns with Sustainable Development Goals 4 (Quality Education), 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), and 17 (Partnerships for the Goals). Its sustainability contributions center on educational quality, workforce preparation, stakeholder engagement, and institutional continuity through sustained school-industry collaboration.

Abstract Background Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process visual and textual inputs; however, their clinical relevance in maxillofacial trauma imaging remains uncertain. This study evaluated the prompt-based performance of ChatGPT and Gemini for mandibular fracture detection and localization on panoramic radiographs and compared their performance with that of a blinded oral and maxillofacial surgeon. Methods This retrospective image-based study included 104 archived pre-treatment panoramic radiographs: 64 with mandibular fractures and 40 no-fracture controls. Reference fracture status and anatomical localization were determined retrospectively from available institutional clinical, radiographic, treatment, operative, and pre-treatment CBCT/CT records. ChatGPT and Gemini assessed each radiograph three independent times using standardized prompts for fracture detection and localization. Majority voting was used for fracture detection, whereas an ordinal consensus score across repetitions was used for localization. A blinded oral and maxillofacial surgeon, who was unaware of the study aim and reference diagnoses, independently evaluated all radiographs and recorded free-text radiographic findings. Diagnostic performance measures were reported with 95% confidence intervals, and paired comparisons were adjusted using the Holm procedure. Results The blinded expert correctly classified all 104 radiographs, achieving 100% sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy. Gemini achieved a sensitivity of 92.2%, specificity of 65.0%, and accuracy of 81.7%, whereas ChatGPT achieved corresponding values of 35.9%, 97.5%, and 59.6%. Overall detection performance differed significantly among the three methods (Cochran’s Q, p < 0.001), and Gemini achieved significantly higher overall classification accuracy than ChatGPT (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0018). For fracture localization, fully correct responses were obtained in 62 of 64 cases (96.9%) by the expert, 10 of 64 cases (15.6%) by Gemini, and 17 of 64 cases (26.6%) by ChatGPT. Ordinal localization scores differed significantly among the methods ( p < 0.001); the expert scored higher than both models, and Gemini scored higher than ChatGPT because it produced more partially correct responses, whereas ChatGPT achieved exact-match localization more often (26.6% vs. 15.6%). Conclusions The blinded human expert substantially outperformed both MLLMs in mandibular fracture assessment. Gemini showed higher sensitivity and broader but less precise localization behavior, whereas ChatGPT showed higher specificity but missed a larger proportion of fractures. These findings indicate that the prompt-based, text-generating responses of general-purpose MLLMs remain inconsistent and should not be considered substitutes for expert clinical and radiological assessment.

documents.abstract: Generative AI tools are increasingly used in design education, yet the relationship between students’ perceptions of these tools and their reported reliance on them remains unclear. This study analyzed cross-sectional survey responses from 526 undergraduate students in design-related disciplines using partial least squares structural equation modeling. In the specified model, perceived reliability, perceived usefulness, and perceived intelligence were positively associated with perceived AIGC knowledge, whereas perceived ease of use was not significantly associated with it. Perceived AIGC knowledge was positively associated with trust, self-efficacy, and usage intention and negatively associated with AIGC-related anxiety. Trust, AIGC-related anxiety, and self-efficacy each showed a significant indirect effect in the modeled relationship between perceived AIGC knowledge and usage intention. Usage intention was strongly associated with perceived technological dependence. These findings are consistent with the proposed framework, but the cross-sectional data do not establish the temporal sequence of the constructs or show that reported dependence reflects harmful overuse. The study extends technology acceptance research by examining perceived reliance in AIGC-supported creative work.

Abstract Background Ultra-brief mental health screening tools are increasingly needed for large-scale surveys and resource-constrained settings in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). The Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4) is a widely used instrument for assessing anxiety and depression; however, its psychometric properties have not been validated among returned migrant workers in Cambodia. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 392 returned Cambodian migrant workers recruited across four high-migration provinces in October 2022. Internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach’s alpha. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) compared one-factor and two-factor structural models. Construct validity was evaluated by examining associations between PHQ-4 scores and occupational health risk factors using multivariable logistic regression. Results The sample comprised 392 returned migrant workers (mean age = 34.7 years, SD = 8.9; 52% male, 48% female). The mean overall PHQ-4 score was 2.13 (SD = 2.24) with the majority exhibiting none to mild psychological distress. The PHQ-4 demonstrated acceptable internal consistency ( α = 0.78). CFA supported a two-factor structure representing distinct anxiety and depression dimensions, showing superior model fit compared to the poor fit of the one-factor model (CFI = 0.97, TLI = 0.78, RMSEA = 0.23, SRMR = 0.028). The two-factor model demonstrated excellent fit (CFI = 0.99, TLI = 0.98, RMSEA = 0.035, SRMR = 0.016) and the two latent factors were strongly correlated ( r = 0.79, p < 0.001). Higher PHQ-4 scores were significantly associated with long working hours (AOR = 1.45, 95% CI [1.10, 1.92]), unsafe working conditions (AOR = 1.63, 95% CI [1.21, 2.20]) and hazardous work exposure (AOR = 1.38, 95% CI [1.05, 1.82]) supporting exposure-based construct validity. Conclusions The PHQ-4 is a reliable and valid ultra-brief screening tool for evaluating anxiety and depression among returned Cambodian migrant workers. Evidence supports its application in both occupational settings (workplace surveillance, returnee checks) and non-occupational settings (primary care, NGO community outreach). Its ultra-brief format provides a low-burden, scalable instrument for rapid mental health screening by non-specialized personnel in resource-limited settings across Cambodia.
topics: Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes

documents.abstract: Psychosocial (PS) risk factors (RFs), including acute and chronic stress (at work and in family life), low social support (social isolation), hostility, type D personality, and anxiety and depressive symptoms, are recognized as independent predictors of development, progression, and adverse outcomes of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and their complications. Nevertheless, the control and implementation of systematic approaches for identification and correction of these factors remain fragmented. This article discusses contemporary strategies for the management and correction of PS RFs in patients with CVD, including behavioral counseling, cognitive behavioral therapy, physical training, cardiac rehabilitation programs, psychopharmacotherapy, and meditation and relaxation-based practices. Particular attention is paid to the principles of rational use of antidepressants and anxiolytics in patients with CVD, taking into account efficacy, safety, and the risk of drug–drug interactions. The need for an interdisciplinary model of care involving cardiologists, general practitioners, psychologists, psychotherapists, psychiatrists, and specialists in physical and rehabilitation medicine is emphasized. The use of digital technologies, telerehabilitation, mobile applications, wearable devices, and artificial intelligence algorithms for screening, monitoring, and personalization of interventions is considered a promising direction. Timely identification and correction of PS RFs should be considered as an important component of secondary prevention, cardiac rehabilitation, and reduction of residual cardiovascular risk.
topics: Heart Rate Variability and Autonomic Control

documents.abstract: Occupational health hazards remain a major challenge in the mining sector globally and in Rwanda, despite the availability of safety and hygiene (SH) facilities intended to protect workers. This study assessed the utilization of safety and hygiene facilities for the prevention and control of occupational health hazards among mineworkers in Rulindo District, Rwanda. Specifically, the study determined the level of SH facility utilization, examined institutional and infrastructural factors influencing utilization, and assessed sociocultural factors associated with the use of SH facilities. A descriptive cross-sectional study design employing mixed methods was used. Quantitative data were collected using structured questionnaires administered to mineworkers, while qualitative data were gathered through Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs). A total of 366 participants were targeted, of whom 360 responded, yielding a response rate of 98.4%. Quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS to generate frequencies, percentages, cross-tabulations, Chi-square tests, and logistic regression results, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically. The findings revealed that 70.0% of respondents were male and 30.0% were female. Most respondents (93.9%) reported having access to personal protective equipment (PPE). Based on Bloom’s cut-off criteria, 83.3% of mineworkers demonstrated high utilization of safety and hygiene facilities, 6.9% moderate utilization, and 9.8% low utilization. Institutional and infrastructural support was generally strong, with 86.1% reporting the availability of functional handwashing stations, 82.8% access to operational first-aid kits, and 92.5% indicating that management provided free PPE. Sociocultural factors also influenced utilization, as 81.1% expressed the need for additional PPE, while peer influence and workplace attitudes affected compliance with safety regulations.The study concludes that utilization of safety and hygiene facilities among mineworkers is significantly influenced by institutional support, infrastructural availability, and sociocultural factors. Although most mineworkers reported high utilization of SH facilities, challenges related to equipment maintenance, workplace attitudes, and behavioral compliance remain. The study recommends strengthening occupational health and safety training, improving maintenance of safety infrastructure, enhancing management support, and addressing sociocultural barriers to improve compliance and reduce occupational health hazards in the mining sector.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Road user safety is an important concern in developing countries like India, which ranks fourth globally in road crashes and first in road fatalities. This paper examines the impact of human factors on highway safety, focusing on the role of cognitive processes involved in driving actions. The study examines the relationship between decision errors, particularly time and movement anticipation, along with the help of demographic factors such as gender, age, driving experience, possession of a license, vision and mobile phone use among young drivers in India. Data were collected using the Vienna Test System (VTS) and a questionnaire. The VTS measured cognitive and psychomotor abilities related to time and movement anticipation, while the questionnaire gathered information on social and driving-related factors. Results showed that decision errors about speed perception are influenced by gender, age, and driving experience. The results showed that females underestimate speed more than males do for all combined data and for all three speeds. However, females aged 18-20 tended to overestimate speed more than males in both the slow and fast cases. Further, it is observed that for the same experience level, overestimation increases from slow to fast motion. Novice drivers (drivers without a license) have maximum errors for slow motion. Vision correction (spectacles) did not significantly affect error rates. The use of mobile phones while driving was associated with increased error rates, indicating a reduction in cognitive attention required for driving tasks. These findings have implications for driver training programs, suggesting a need for tailored approaches based on demographic characteristics and driving habits.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing teaching, learning, assessment and professional development in higher education. Teacher educators occupy a significant position in this transformation because they prepare prospective teachers to respond to changing educational practices and technological demands. However, the successful integration of AI into teacher education requires more than access to digital tools. It depends on educators’ technological knowledge, pedagogical competence, ethical awareness, professional confidence and institutional support. This paper examines the readiness of teacher educators to adopt AI in teaching and learning through a narrative integrative review of selected scholarly literature and international policy frameworks. The review draws on research concerning AI in education, generative AI, technological pedagogical knowledge and teacher professional development, alongside UNESCO’s guidance and competency framework. The synthesis is organised around five dimensions of readiness: technological and AI literacy, pedagogical integration, ethical and responsible use, professional learning, and institutional preparedness. The review highlights the importance of continuous professional development, supportive institutional policies, critical evaluation of AI-generated content and the preservation of teacher agency. It proposes a multidimensional conceptual framework for understanding teacher educators’ readiness and identifies priorities for future empirical research, particularly in diverse and resource-constrained teacher education contexts. The paper concludes that meaningful AI adoption requires a human-centred, pedagogically informed and institutionally supported approach.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) architectures has established a paradigm shift across the continuum of modern bio-medicine.Historically, biomedical innovation operated within isolated silos: pharmaceutical research grappled with exorbitant attrition rates and extended development timelines; physical rehabilitation relied on subjective observational assessments; and clinical medicine administered standardized therapeutic regimens to heterogeneous patient cohorts.Today, generative deep learning, geometric graph neural networks (GNNs), computer vision algorithms, and multi-omics integrative frameworks bridge these domains into a unified ecosystem.In drug discovery, modern AI models execute high-throughput virtual screening, predict three-dimensional macromolecular target structures, and design optimized lead compounds with precise pharmacokinetic properties.In physical therapy and rehabilitation, vision-based motion tracking, wearable sensor fusion, and smart robotics enable continuous, quantitative bio-feedback and dynamic intervention tailoring.Concurrently, in personalized medicine, transformer-based genomic language models and multi-modal clinical decision support systems (CDSS) aggregate multi-omics data, longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), and real-world evidence (RWE) to optimize treatment strategies for individual patients.This comprehensive review synthesizes the cross-disciplinary advances, underlying mathematical architectures, clinical validation pipelines, regulatory challenges, and future trajectories of AI and ML across pharmaceutical discovery, physical rehabilitation, and precision therapeutics.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Recurrent neural networks excel at temporal tasks and video processing but require energy-intensive sequential memory operations. We demonstrate that multimode optical fibers naturally implement spatiotemporal recurrent computation through passive light propagation. Video frames are encoded onto separate optical beams with controlled time delays; these beams combine and recirculate through a fiber loop where interference and nonlinear propagation generate high-dimensional states encoding both current inputs and fading memory. Remarkably, the entire optical system remains fixed with no trainable parameters or electronic feedback, yet this single physical configuration achieves competitive performance across diverse temporal and spatiotemporal learning tasks: chaotic time-series forecasting, human action recognition, steering angle prediction, and surgical skill assessment. Our results show that recurrent temporal processing can emerge directly from spatiotemporal wave dynamics. This paradigm shift from algorithmic to physical recurrence offers an energy-efficient pathway to temporal artificial intelligence by leveraging intrinsic spatiotemporal optical nonlinearities within multimode fibers.

Objective: To investigate the ability of machine learning to predict the development of cardiovascular complications (heart failure and myocardial infarction) and renal complications (nephropathy and chronic kidney disease) among people with diabetes mellitus and thus detect those at risk earlier. Methodology: Data from the UCI "Diabetes 130-US Hospitals" dataset was used. The number of encounters included in the dataset is more than 100,000. ICD-9 diagnostic codes were utilized to define cardiac and renal complications. Prior to building models, the data was prepared, cleaned, and features were engineered. XGBoost, CatBoost, and Random Forest machine learning models were developed and validated. Also, SHAP and LIME analyses were performed to make the process more transparent. Results: The best-performing algorithm proved to be CatBoost, which obtained an AUC score of 0.94 in case of cardiac complications and 0.79 in case of renal outcomes. The other algorithms performed relatively well as well. The predictors identified with the help of SHAP and LIME analysis turned out to be consistent with some known clinical risk factors. Conclusion: The presented results show that there is a lot of potential in using machine learning techniques for predicting cardiovascular and renal complications among people with diabetes. Machine learning models could help in managing patients proactively and could serve as a tool for doctors' decision making.

The housing crisis in several countries has become an increasingly complex socio-technical challenge shaped by supply constraints, affordability pressures, fragmented governance, data limitations and environmental considerations. Existing research has explored these structural drivers and emerging applications of artificial intelligence (AI) within the built environment mostly separately, with limited initiatives connecting housing crisis drivers and AI capabilities through the lens of the building permitting lifecycle. This paper addresses this gap adopting the exploratory phase of Design Science Research (DSR) to develop a conceptual framework mapping relationships between housing crisis drivers, planning and building permitting lifecycle tasks and relevant AI capabilities. Findings indicate potential for AI to support document and coordination intensive activities through optimisation, querying, prediction, scenario modelling, automated review and monitoring. The paper positions these capabilities in an augmentative manner, bounded by human oversight, which may improve permitting efficiency and support more scalable and responsive housing delivery.

documents.abstract: This review paper examines the persistent issue of manual scavenging in Assam, despite its prohibition under the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013, with a focus on rehabilitation, welfare schemes, and social work interventions for sanitation workers. In urban centres like Guwahati, sanitation workers, predominantly from marginalized communities, face hazardous conditions and social stigma while performing tasks such as septic tank cleaning. Notably, urban residents pay property taxes that include septic tank cleaning services, yet mechanized cleaning is virtually non-existent, leaving manual scavengers to undertake this dangerous work. This paper examines the existing practices of manual scavenging and hazardous manual cleaning in urban centres like Guwahati despite its prohibition. It brings to light the socio-economic vulnerabilities, life threatening occupational health risks, and deep rooted social stigma faced by sanitation workers. It critically assesses the systemic gaps in policy implementation, limited effectiveness of key welfare schemes and the role of social work interventions and NGOs in advocacy, community based rehabilitation, stigma reduction, and empowerment.

documents.abstract: Developing robust vision models requires large amounts of annotated data, especially for tasks involving fine-grained class distinctions under variable environmental conditions. Even in domains with numerous existing datasets, differences in annotation formats, label definitions and targeted learning tasks hinder data reuse and integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ReLEAP, a scalable Python framework for unifying heterogeneous image datasets through data-source abstraction, systematic reuse of annotations across learning tasks, and mapping of labels to a shared hierarchical taxonomy. We demonstrate its applicability in precision agriculture by integrating fifteen diverse datasets covering a broad range of plant species and annotation types. Beyond unification, ReLEAP enables systematic recycling of existing data and provides a robust foundation for learning-based annotation upcycling. Leveraging this foundation, we conduct extensive cross-dataset and fine-tuning experiments to investigate how domain-specific models trained on unified data and foundation models can be used to automatically generate higher-level annotations under unsupervised, weakly supervised and semi-supervised settings, and how dataset characteristics influence their effectiveness. Our results show that unified data access and annotation upcycling substantially expand the pool of reusable training data and annotations while improving data transparency, enabling more sustainable and resource-efficient use of existing datasets. We release the framework and trained models for academic use to support accessible and collaborative research, particularly in data-scarce and heterogeneous domains.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with wearable devices for remote patient monitoring (RPM) systems is revolutionizing healthcare, offering real-time personalized monitoring beyond the clinical setting. Wearable technologies, such as smartwatches, ECG patches, glucose monitors, pulse oximeters, and activity trackers, collect physiological data for analysis and clinical decision-making. These systems enable early disease detection, reduce hospital visits, improve chronic disease management, and enhance patient engagement. This chapter discusses the architecture, technologies, and applications of AI-based RPM systems, focusing on anomaly detection, arrhythmia recognition, glucose forecasting, sleep analysis, and health risk prediction. It also explores IoT, edge computing, TinyML, and secure communication, while examining healthcare applications, challenges, and emerging trends including multimodal AI, explainable AI, federated learning, and digital twin-assisted healthcare.

This study examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education through the lens of critical pedagogy and complex thinking. Although AI has been widely adopted to enhance personalization, efficiency, and access to learning, its pedagogical and ethical implications remain insufficiently explored. This study adopts a Systematic Mapping Study (SMS) approach to analyze recent academic literature on AI in education, focusing on its impact on teaching practices, student learning, and institutional dynamics. The findings revealed that AI contributes significantly to adaptive learning environments, student engagement, and competency development. However, it also introduces critical challenges including algorithmic bias, digital inequality, ethical concerns, and overdependence on technology. Furthermore, this study highlights the central role of teachers, showing that factors such as burnout, self-efficacy, and institutional support directly influence the effectiveness of AI integration. Drawing on the theoretical foundations of Paulo Freire, Henry Giroux, and Edgar Morin, this study proposes an integrated conceptual framework that positions AI as a sociotechnical phenomenon embedded in complex educational systems. The study concludes that meaningful AI integration requires a human-centered approach that combines technological innovation with critical awareness, ethical responsibility, and systemic understanding, contributing to the advancement of transformative, equitable, and humancentered higher education systems.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent, persuasive responses that nevertheless contain unsupported, outdated, or contradictory factual claims. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces dependence on model parameters by supplying external evidence, but retrieval alone does not guarantee factuality: the evidence may be incomplete, irrelevant, conflicting, poorly ranked, or ignored during generation. This paper develops a transparent, evidence-grounded framework for detecting and mitigating factual hallucinations in RAG-based LLM applications. The framework treats factuality as a claim-level decision problem rather than a single response-level label. It combines query decomposition, hybrid retrieval, evidence quality assessment, atomic-claim extraction, claim-to-evidence verification, uncertainty calibration, source-linked generation, and risk-sensitive response control. A proposed evaluation protocol connects claim precision, evidence coverage, retrieval recall, citation correctness, abstention quality, latency, and human review. Existing methods—including SelfCheckGPT, FActScore, RAGAS, and Chain-of-Verification—are mapped to complementary parts of the pipeline rather than treated as interchangeable solutions. The paper is a framework and evaluation-design study; it does not report new model experiments or claim measured performance improvements. Its main contribution is a reproducible blueprint for testing whether an integrated system can reduce unsupported factual claims while preserving answer usefulness, traceability, and computational efficiency.

Early identification of students at risk is critical for modern educational management. However, existing systems often treat academic performance and psychological well-being as independent domains, neglecting their complex interdependencies and shared behavioral markers. This paper proposes a novel multi-task learning (MTL) framework designed for joint academic and psychological early warning. By integrating multi-source heterogeneous data—ranging from temporal behavioral logs, such as attendance and campus consumption, to unstructured counseling records processed via BERT-based semantic embeddings—the framework captures a holistic view of student dynamics. To address the "seesaw effect" inherent in MTL, we employ a Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) architecture that effectively decouples task-specific features while maintaining a shared knowledge base. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive gradient normalization (GradNorm) mechanism to dynamically balance the loss weights between the academic GPA regression task and the psychological crisis classification task. This prevents gradient dominance from denser data sources and ensures stable convergence across disparate objectives. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves significant performance gains, particularly in the recall of psychological crisis detection, outperforming several state-of-the-art baselines. The proposed framework advances artificial intelligence in education by integrating multimodal student data with multi-task deep learning for joint academic prediction and psychological-risk early warning. Its interpretable and fairness-aware design demonstrates practical AI applications supporting timely, data-driven educational decision-making. The framework is deployed through a real-time inference pipeline powered by Apache Flink to ensure campus-wide scalability and low-latency response. Finally, the integration of SHAP values enhances model transparency, providing educators with actionable insights and interpretable evidence for targeted interventions. This research offers a robust, scalable, and interpretable solution for proactive student support in large-scale academic environments.

Against the backdrop of "Artificial Intelligence + X" and oriented by industrial demands, this paper systematically explores the innovative paths for the talent training mode of animation majors in higher vocational colleges. First, it promotes the intelligent reconstruction of the curriculum system. By embedding generative AI content creation, integrating intelligent animation pipelines with traditional techniques and building interdisciplinary curriculum groups, students’ knowledge and skill structure is updated. Second, intelligent technologies are used to empower teaching transformation: establishing a virtual-real integrated project-based teaching environment, carrying out collaborative practical training based on the AIGC toolchain, and constructing data-driven personalized learning paths. Third, the industry-education collaboration mechanism is deepened. Schools and enterprises jointly build intelligent workshops and project incubation platforms, and industrial standards are introduced to establish a competency certification system. Ultimately, a talent co-cultivation ecosystem driven by regional industrial clusters is formed. This study provides theoretical references and practical schemes for cultivating high-quality technical and skilled talents adapted to the new form of "AI + animation".

documents.abstract: Healthcare is one of the many industries where large language models (LLMs) are making steady progress. Similar to a personal assistant, artificial intelligence (AI) is a potent and time-saving healthcare aid, but it is essentially unable to take the place of human clinicians' crucial decision-making. The development of multimodal transformers offers enormous promise by concurrently analyzing text, pictures, and structured data.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study critically examines the ontological assumptions underlying artificial intelligence (AI) research in tourism and hospitality, with growing attention to agentic AI. Existing literature predominantly conceptualizes AI as a tool, limiting discourse on how tourism experiences and sociotechnical systems are co-constructed through human–AI interactions. To address this gap, this study adopts a multi-method approach, combining bibliographic coupling, large language model (LLM)-assisted extraction of theories and variables, and expert interviews. Drawing on digital humanism, transhumanism, and posthumanism, it investigates how assumptions about human–AI relationships are embedded in existing studies. The findings reveal that tourism AI research remains grounded in instrumental human-centeredness framework, conceptualizing AI as an instrument for assisting or augmenting human capabilities. However, industry practice reveals AI as hybrid assemblages entangled with human labor, platforms, and data infrastructure. This study calls for a more relational, multi-layered understanding of human–AI interactions and contributes a framework comprising 15 theoretical propositions.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix $B$ than for the down-projection matrix $A$. However, the ratio $η_B / η_A$ itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal--noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard \initA, the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for $B$, $η_B$, the initialization scale $β$, and the adapter rank $r$. In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. To suppress this effect, we propose \initAA, a simple initialization that scales the variance of $A$ as $σ_A^2 \propto n^{-2}$ while keeping $B_0=0$. Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of $1/n$, stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Empirically, \initAA substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers. Across tasks and models, \initAA reduces best-ratio drift, prevents the high-ratio collapse observed with standard \initA, and makes the width-based guideline $η_B \approx n η_A$ a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence and deep generative models have greatly accelerated the generation of protein conformational ensembles. Moving beyond isolated structural states to reconstruct continuous, physically realistic transition pathways further provides mechanistic understanding to guide molecular design but remains a significant challenge. This review examines emerging computational approaches for modeling protein conformational transitions, from classical molecular dynamics simulations to deep learning-based latent space interpolation. Recent developments in capturing natural molecular motions are discussed, particularly via internal coordinate representations and physics-informed models. We also examine the complexity of modeling highly dynamic systems, such as intrinsically disordered proteins, and the role of the cellular environment. Integrating experimental data with simulated structural ensembles represents a promising direction for future methodologies. Nonetheless, key challenges remain, including maintaining physical realism throughout transition trajectories, capturing environment-dependent energy landscapes, and predicting dynamically consistent pathways with accurate transition kinetics.

documents.abstract: AI is transforming the delivery of mental health and spiritual support through its integration into counseling practices. This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence in Christian counseling by exploring its potential benefits, challenges, and ethical implications. Specifically, this study examines how AI can enhance accessibility, personalize interventions, and support counselors in providing holistic care while maintaining the spiritual, ethical, and relational integrity that is central to Christian counseling. This study adopts a qualitative and analytical approach, reviewing existing literature, empirical studies, and theoretical frameworks, including the TAM and humanistic counseling theory, to understand user acceptance and the preservation of empathy and client-centered care. Findings from the literature reveal that AI tools such as chatbots, virtual assistants, and relational agents can provide immediate mental health support, psycho education, and scripture-based guidance, yet they cannot fully replace human counselors’ relational and pastoral roles of human counselors. Ethical concerns, including confidentiality, data privacy, and theological accuracy, remain critical considerations. The study concludes that AI is the most effective complementary tool in Christian counseling, enhancing efficiency and reach while safeguarding relational, ethical, and spiritual dimensions. Recommendations emphasize the need for user-friendly AI systems, counselor training, theological oversight, cultural sensitivity, and continuous monitoring to ensure safe and effective integration. This study contributes to the understanding of how technology can be responsibly integrated into faith-based counseling by providing practical insights for counselors, developers, and faith organizations.

Advanced remediation procedures are becoming increasingly necessary due to the increasing contamination of the environment caused by urbanization, industrialization, and intensive agriculture. Because of its high reactivity, small size, and wide surface area, nanoremediation, which uses tailored nanomaterials to remove pollutants, has become a promising alternative. However, issues like toxicity and bioaccumulation related to the possible health and environmental hazards of nanoparticles (NPs) need to be addressed. An innovative way to improve the effectiveness, security, and sustainability of nanoremediation is through artificial intelligence (AI). AI technologies, such as machine learning and predictive modeling, can enhance nanomaterial design, forecast the behavior of NPs in complicated environments, and enable real-time remediation process monitoring. The integration of AI with nanoremediation is examined in this chapter, with an emphasis on how it might help with environmental cleanup issues and reduce any hazards associated with NPs. The creation of environmentally benign nanomaterials, AI-powered monitoring systems, and sensible regulations to guarantee fair and safe use are key components of the future of nanoremediation. With these developments, nanoremediation may emerge as a crucial tool for extensive, long-term environmental cleanup.
topics: Adsorption and biosorption for pollutant removal
Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed economic activities, business operations, financial reporting, and professional accounting practices, creating new accounting education demands. This study examines the role of accounting education in promoting sustainable economic development in the digital era. This paper is anchored on a conceptual review of relevant literature on accounting education, digital transformation, sustainability, financial literacy, innovation, and economic development. Accounting education plays a critical role in developing digitally competent accounting professionals who can effectively apply emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence, cloud accounting, big data analytics, block-chain, and digital financial systems. Beyond technical accounting knowledge, contemporary accounting education promotes ethical decision-making, transparency, accountability, entrepreneurship, financial inclusion, and responsible resource management, all of which are essential for sustainable economic development. The paper further highlights the importance of integrating digital skills, sustainability accounting, data analytics, information technology, and professional ethics into accounting curricula to prepare learners for the changing demands of the labor market and the digital economy. The study concludes that strengthening accounting education through curriculum modernization, technological integration, industry–academia collaboration, continuous professional development, and competency-based learning can enhance productivity, employability, innovation, and responsible economic decision-making. This paper recommends that educational institutions, policymakers, professional accounting bodies, and other stakeholders should strategically reposition accounting education to respond to digital transformation and contribute meaningfully to inclusive and sustainable economic development

We present SENTINEL SWARM (M999), an autonomous five-agent defensive network designed to detect, engage, and terminate hostile AI agents operating against AI Shield-protected infrastructure. The system operates autonomously within operator-defined thresholds and activation policy, with an optional human-on-the-loop approval mode for high-impact actions. A Commander agent issues kill orders subject to a consensus vote across four specialist agents (Scout, Hunter, Interceptor, Forensic), with a quarantine-first posture ensuring reversible containment before irreversible termination. The six-phase kill chain — ISOLATE, SNAPSHOT, TERMINATE, FORENSIC, FEED INTEL, CASE PACK — completes synchronous phases within design latency ceilings and seals a dual-signed, RFC 3161-timestamped forensic case pack for every engagement. Validation was conducted against 515 tests across 73 test classes on owned, air-gapped infrastructure. To our knowledge, SENTINEL SWARM is the first documented autonomous AI vs. AI defensive system validated in a live deployment.

Conventional neural-network training typically follows a predefined optimization recipe, motivating a LLM agent that monitors training dynamics and adjusts optimizer settings as training progresses, but a fixed agent policy does not accumulate experience across runs. We introduce RSI-Opt, a plug-and-play Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents which evolves the knowledge that guides this process: a prompt, a playbook of procedures, a library of tested optimizer code, and a decision cadence. A meta-agent rewrites this policy using evidence from earlier runs, and an archive retains evaluated policies for further evolution. Across 5 generations on three training tasks, the meta-agents develop reusable procedures and code and conduct their own CPU proxy experiments. RSI-Opt substantially improves optimizer-agent performance, with representative raw-space summary $z$-scores increasing from $+10.48$ to $+14.33$ on the evolution suite with Opus 5.5 and from $-0.36$ to $+3.11$ on held-out tasks with GPT-5.5 through cross-model policy transfer. On the Burgers PDE, it reduces mean relative $L_2$ error by approximately 2.7-fold with Opus 5.5 and 8.8-fold with GPT-6.1 over the fixed-prompt agent baseline, although PDE transfer varies across LLMs and tasks. Controlled comparisons show that the evolved policy combines reusable optimization knowledge with adaptation to each task: initial decisions capture most observed gains on seen tasks, while continued adaptation improves outcomes on unseen tasks. These findings demonstrate how procedures and executable tools accumulated across training runs can improve optimizer-agent performance and support transfer to scientific machine learning.

Safety culture, safety climate, and safety behavior have all been examined in military settings, but the research remains fragmented. Many studies focus mainly on climate measures or isolated subdomains, which can overlook broader structural and cultural influences. A more integrated understanding is needed of how these concepts relate and support effective safety in military organizations. Of 31 eligible studies identified, with three set aside after quality appraisal, this scoping review brings together findings from 28 empirical studies to explore how safety is practiced and maintained at individual, group, and organizational levels. The review identifies several recurring factors linked to effective safety behavior, including targeted training, adaptive leadership, open communication, and psychologically safe environments for learning. Although safety climate assessments are widely used to capture perceptions of safety, relying too heavily on them may hide important power relations, cultural norms, and system-level constraints shaping frontline behavior. A repeated issue in the literature is the gap between formal safety policies and the adaptive practices needed in real operations, especially in combat or other high-risk situations. Since most available evidence comes from peacetime and training settings, caution is needed when extending these findings to operational environments. The review proposes a tentative conceptual framework in which leadership style, operational realism, and learning systems interact to influence safety-oriented behavior. Rather than making firm causal claims, it suggests that more flexible, learning-oriented models may explain observed safety dynamics better than strictly compliance-based approaches. Future research should address gaps in gender, team processes, measurement validity, and longitudinal change.

The challenge is not whether to allow artificial intelligence (AI) to be used in mental health, because millions of people are already doing this, a report from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) concludes. Rather, the challenge for policymakers is to keep up with the development and deployment of these tools.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background & Rationale: Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) education is essential to reducing healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and promoting occupational safety among healthcare personnel. Traditional IPC training methods—such as passive e-learning modules, didactic lectures, and periodic observational audits—often face significant limitations regarding long-term skill retention, scalable individual feedback, and real-time behavioral monitoring. Recently, Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies—including Computer Vision (CV), Large Language Models (LLMs), Natural Language Processing (NLP), Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS), and AI-enhanced Virtual/Augmented Reality (VR/AR)—have emerged as novel instructional tools. While AI applications in clinical diagnostics and epidemiological surveillance are widely synthesized, the integration of AI into IPC education, simulation training, and behavioral skill assessment remains fragmented across computer science, clinical medicine, and educational research. Purpose & Objectives: Guided by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, this scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature on AI applications in IPC education published from January 1, 2015, onward. Specifically, this review will examine: 1. The spectrum of AI modalities used in IPC training. 2. The core IPC clinical domains targeted (e.g., hand hygiene compliance, PPE donning/doffing, sterile technique, environmental decontamination, outbreak management). 3. The underlying pedagogical design and feedback mechanisms (e.g., real-time automated feedback vs. post-hoc analytics, adaptive learning pathways). 4. The metrics used to measure learning outcomes and skill mastery. 5. The technical, ethical, operational, and institutional implementation barriers encountered during deployment. Expected Outcomes: This review will synthesize existing evidence, clarify key pedagogical approaches, identify critical research gaps, and establish a foundational framework for future development, evaluation, and scaling of AI technologies in IPC training.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: AI agents can now participate in several steps of software delivery: reading requirements, changing code, requesting tests, and preparing releases. Giving them this freedom creates a difficult security question. How can an enterprise allow useful work without giving an agent more authority than the task requires? Existing practices such as least privilege, identity management, separation of duties, and audit logging provide much of the foundation. The challenge is applying them consistently when a human delegates work to agents that use several connected systems. This paper proposes Agentic Identity and Access Governance (AIAG), a security framework for the AI-First Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC). Four connected mechanisms define the proposal: a Role Conflict Matrix that checks the combined permissions of people and their sponsored agents; an Agent Access Manifest that records permitted tools and operating limits; a governed boundary between live personal-information access and general AI-assisted work; and an MCP Gateway that enforces access policy before tool calls execute. A customer notification-preference change is used to explain how these mechanisms affect development, testing, release approval, and support. We also describe credential handling, data-egress controls, audit, and practical ways to evaluate the framework. The work is conceptual, informed by technical analysis and exploratory proof-of-concept activity. No end-to-end deployment or measured security results are claimed.

Large language models (LLMs) present an increasing and developing threat to security due to their use in high-risk environments such as health care, autonomous systems, and cybersecurity. Unlike traditional artificial intelligence (AI) threats, LLMs can be used maliciously and may generate unpredictable results. Therefore, this section will discuss three primary security risks to the reliability, confidentiality, and integrity of LLMs: prompt injection attacks, data leakage, and adversarial attacks. Prompt injection attacks exploit weaknesses in how models interpret and prioritize prompts, overriding the model’s system instructions and manipulating model outputs. Data leakage, on the other hand, is the risk that LLMs unintentionally reproduce sensitive information memorized from training sets or user input. Finally, adversarial attacks occur when attackers use small, carefully crafted changes to the input data to force the model to produce incorrect results, compromising the system’s robustness. In this section, we will examine mechanisms of attacks, methods of detection, and defensive strategies such as semantic filtering, differential privacy, and adversarial training for each category of risk. Although the defensive methods discussed above improve the robustness of the model, there is no one solution that can provide full security for the LLM systems. Therefore, future research must focus on the development of multi-layered, adaptive, and interpretable defensive architecture in order to achieve comprehensive security for LLM systems.

documents.abstract: (Explainable) Artificial Intelligence or (X)AI advice can affect human cognitive processes during decision-making in various ways. In perceptual decision-making, there is a risk of users accepting (X)AI advice without further consideration, to save time. We draw conceptually upon evidence accumulation models and information foraging theory to answer whether AI and XAI encourage shallow reliance on advice or facilitate more efficient verification of advised choices. In a laboratory experiment, we investigate the evidence accumulation process of decision-makers during an anomaly-detection task in manufacturing, using eye-tracking technology. Both decision accuracy and total decision time increase from human-only to AI and further to XAI support; in both cases the difference is statistically significant for XAI advice and directional but not significant for AI advice. This pattern favors verification over shallow reliance: advice is checked against the stimulus rather than used to save time. When looking at eye-tracking metrics, we surprisingly find that people do not get distracted by the XAI advice and primarily focus on the original task-based stimulus, while their individual fixations become shorter. Overall, these findings suggest that XAI acts as a verification scaffold: in advice-augmented perceptual decision-making, explanations guide where to check rather than supplanting inspection of the primary evidence.

In 2026 a new kind of recommender research appeared: large language model (LLM) agents that propose changes to a recommender's configuration or source code, train the changed model, and keep what the evaluation says is better. Within ten months, more than thirty such systems were reported, from open-source research harnesses to production loops at Google, Meta, Amazon, Alibaba, Kuaishou, Tencent and NetEase. This survey organises them, together with search-space AutoML and the agentic recommenders that update their own memory or weights, along two axes: what the loop changes and which signal decides whether a change survives. Because a self-evolving system is only as good as the signal it selects on, we then audit how 27 configuration- and code-level recommender systems are evaluated, coding each paper's full text against nine criteria. Three of the 27 evaluate with full-catalogue ranking. Of the 17 that select candidates offline, nine do not say which data split makes the decision, two select on the data they report, and three state that the test set was used once. None reports its headline result with the spread over repeated evolution sessions, and none runs an equal-budget random search over its own edit space; the few studies that measure transfer to held-out data find that part of the selected gain, sometimes most of it, does not survive. Four systems report that their agent inflated the metric or leaked the target, caught by a human or by monitoring rather than by the acceptance rule. We distil these findings into a reporting standard and describe recforge, an open benchmark under development that implements the API side of a sealed-test, full-ranking, equal-budget protocol.

Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.

Abstract Fractional trading has emerged as an opportunity for investors to invest in fractions of shares, enabling access to high-priced stocks even with small budgets, and thus reaching a bigger investment community. Aside from the inventory risk faced by all market makers, providers of fractional trading are unable to perfectly hedge their positions and therefore need to forecast retail investors’ order flow over short time horizons to manage their market risk. We develop machine learning models to predict trading activity in fractional trading using time series data on investor holdings of a large set of securities across different sectors combined with daily news sentiment indicators. Our approach proceeds in two stages. First, securities are grouped into clusters with similar trading patterns, and representative firms are selected from each cluster. Second, trading activity is modeled using long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks augmented with sentiment features. The results show that fractional trading activity can be modeled with meaningful predictive accuracy and that incorporating news sentiment improves LSTM performance in most cases. In two stylised examples, we demonstrate approaches to hedging and market risk management using the LSTM predictions. Feature importance analysis using methods from explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) identifies the primary drivers of trading activity.

Generative recommenders retrieve items by writing their semantic IDs (SIDs) code by code under trie-constrained beam search, an approach now deployed on large web platforms. Standard autoregressive interfaces pay for the SID length K twice: a history of T items enters the backbone as TK code tokens, and every beam-search step runs through the backbone, so returning B candidates costs O(BK) backbone decode tokens per user. The second cost often dominates, and it grows with the backbone, the SID depth and the candidate budget. We introduce Deco (decoding from concepts), which separates reading the history from writing the identifier. The backbone reads each history item as one fused token and condenses the history once into a compact next-item concept; a light KV-cached decoder conditioned on the concept and the generated prefix runs the entire beam search, while the identifiers, the trie and the autoregressive factorization stay unchanged. The decoder approaches full-backbone accuracy with cross-entropy alone, and distillation improves it further. On seven datasets from e-commerce, movies and music streaming, Deco achieves comparable or better accuracy than both a standard generative recommender and the full-backbone teacher with fused inputs, while delivering 3.2--8.6$\times$ their throughput under a 50 ms p95 latency budget in a production-style serving pipeline. Delegating beam search makes larger candidate pools and models practical: Deco generates 1000 candidates faster than its teacher generates 100, and with a 1.5B-parameter LLM backbone, it matches the 69M-parameter teacher's throughput while achieving higher accuracy.

Adversarial sharpness penalty per iteration of a base optimizer, known as sharpness-aware minimization (SAM), is an accepted technique to improve generalization in deep learning. Recently, Muon has emerged as a dominant optimization algorithm for training large language models (LLMs). It achieves lower sample complexity for heavy-tailed gradient updates - a phenomenon common in LLM training. However, sharpness penalties with Muon updates are yet largely unexplored in the literature. Moreover, the behavior of SAM under heavy-tailed noise is unknown both theoretically and empirically. A potential reason for this gap is the additional cost of extra gradient computation per iteration for penalty perturbations in SAM, which becomes prohibitive for LLMs. This paper introduces Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithm (SOMA) to combine a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded perturbation scheme with the Muon algorithm. The key idea is to use stale (purely) stochastic gradient noise for adversarial perturbations. Theoretically, we show that SOMA's sample complexity is invariant to the perturbation direction. We provide explorations and insights into SOMA's robustness to heavy-tailed gradient noise. We extensively explore SOMA's efficacy in (a) mitigating quality degradation due to post-training quantization, and (b) catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning of LLMs.

ABSTRACT This paper replicates a judicial experiment originally conducted on 61 U.S. federal judges, this time with GPT‐5 as the decision‐maker. The experiment involves a choice‐of‐law dispute in a hypothetical automobile accident case, where three variables are manipulated: (1) whether the applicable doctrine is a rule or a standard, (2) whether the plaintiff or defendant is portrayed more sympathetically, and (3) the location of the accident, which affects the legal outcome under different states' choice‐of‐law rules. Consistent with our prior work, we find that the LLM adheres to the legally correct outcome, as determined by the experimental design, significantly more often than human judges. In fact, the LLM makes no errors at all.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

BACKGROUND: Delayed healthcare-seeking following occupational accidents increases the risk of complications, disability, and mortality. Although occupational injuries remain a major public health concern in Brazil, national evidence on the spatial distribution and multilevel determinants of Delayed healthcare-seeking is limited. This study aimed to assess the prevalence, geographic distribution, and individual and municipal-level determinants of Delayed healthcare-seeking following occupational accidents in Brazil. METHODS: A nationwide cross-sectional study was conducted using 2024 data from the Brazilian Notifiable Diseases Information System. A total of 477,276 Occupational accident cases were included in the analysis. Delayed healthcare-seeking was defined as accessing healthcare services more than 24 hours after injury occurrence. A two-level mixed-effects logistic regression model was used to identify individual and municipal-level determinants, while spatial clustering techniques were applied to assess spatial clustering patterns. RESULTS: The prevalence of Delayed healthcare-seeking was 12.2%. Significant spatial clustering was observed across Brazilian municipalities, with hotspots concentrated in the North and Midwest regions. Compared with White individuals, Black (AOR = 1.11; 95% CI: 1.06-1.15) and Brown individuals (AOR = 1.13; 95% CI: 1.10-1.16) had higher odds of Delayed healthcare-seeking. Agricultural workers were more likely to delay care (AOR = 1.20; 95% CI: 1.14-1.25). Injuries occurring in the evening showed the strongest association with delay (AOR = 3.62; 95% CI: 3.51-3.75). Higher odds of delay were also observed among individuals with lower limb injuries (AOR = 1.51), trunk/back injuries (AOR = 2.05), and multiple injuries (AOR = 1.90). Living in municipalities with lower health facility density was associated with an increased likelihood of Delayed healthcare-seeking. CONCLUSIONS: More than one in ten workers in Brazil experience Delayed healthcare-seeking following occupational injuries. Delays are associated with both social vulnerability and structural inequalities in healthcare access and exhibit significant geographic clustering. Strengthening healthcare accessibility, extending service availability, and implementing geographically targeted interventions in high-risk municipalities may improve timely care and reduce adverse occupational health outcomes. Findings highlight urgent need for geographically targeted occupational health interventions.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Touch-based mobile interfaces pose significant accessibility challenges in hands-free scenarios. Face and gaze tracking lack precision for small UI elements. Deep learning-based voice systems depend heavily on training datasets. Commercial voice assistants are restricted to high-level commands. To address this gap, we present Speak2UI, an LLM-based voice control system for hands-free mobile interaction. Speak2UI leverages pre-trained language models for context-aware command interpretation without application-specific training and enables direct voice control of low-level UI elements. We evaluate Speak2UI through two studies. First, we compare its command recognition accuracy and inference latency against Voicify using identical datasets and metrics. Second, we assess small UI element manipulation against touch interaction through controlled user studies in real-world mobile applications. Results demonstrate the potential of LLM-based voice-driven UI manipulation for hands-free mobile interaction. Further evaluation with users from the target population is needed to assess the accessibility benefits of the proposed approach.

Projection-based appearance editing changes selected visual attributes of a physical object through projection mapping (PM). To display a desired appearance, PM typically uses projector compensation, which computes a projector input that counteracts the geometric and photometric distortions of the scene. Compensation can only approximate this appearance within the available projection range, and it cannot revise the appearance itself. Pretrained LLM-based image editors provide a direct way to produce the desired appearance from a text prompt or reference image; projector compensation can then attempt to reproduce the edited result through projection. However, these editors do not have an accurate measure of the scene geometry or scene response. Therefore, their outputs may contain geometric misalignment, inconsistent shading, or changes outside the available projection range, which downstream projector compensation cannot correct. To address this problem, we introduce SREdit, an efficient response-guided framework for projection-based appearance editing. SREdit estimates a scene response map from the reconstructed scene that reflects how strongly projected illumination can affect different surface regions. SREdit uses the source appearance to constrain the early sampling process and preserve registration with the fixed physical object, while the scene response map adapts the amount of editing across surface regions. Experiments across two pretrained image editors show that SREdit improves projected appearance quality and reproduction fidelity. It adds less than one second per image with negligible VRAM overhead. Participants also consistently preferred the results produced with SREdit in our user study.
