documents.abstract: Predictive Maintenance (PdM) is the model that brings together sensor data as well as systematic data analysis. Industry 4.0 is broadly using PdMs that are improving the applications of digitized information. The monitoring of the conditions of machine parts and various processes is the main goal of PdM because it predicts the occurrence of any possible failures and results in interventions to optimized maintenance. Nevertheless, rotational components employed in robotics are very important in terms of proactive maintenance. The applications of machine learning models to obtain real-time data and predict when a failure may occur long before the breakdown were the subject of our study. The predictive models are highly accurate on possible component malfunctions with a very reasonable accuracy. Random Forest offers a good accuracy of 92% whereas Neural Network model offers a better accuracy of 94%. These models are efficient as evidenced by their performance measures including precision, recall and the F1-score. These indicators focus on the capability of the model to identify timely component failures.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from the periphery of experimental computing to the centre of managerial practice, reshaping how organisations make decisions, allocate resources, engage customers and manage people. Despite the rapid growth of scholarship on the subject, the literature remains fragmented across functional silos, and the opportunities and risks of AI are frequently examined in isolation from one another. This conceptual study synthesises existing literature to examine the role of AI in modern business management and to articulate an integrated understanding of its opportunities and challenges. Drawing on the technology–organisation–environment framework, the resource-based view, dynamic capabilities theory and the automation–augmentation perspective, the paper develops a conceptual model comprising five interrelated components: AI adoption enablers, AI applications across management functions, the dual effects of AI (opportunities and challenges), organisational outcomes, and moderating governance mechanisms. The model proposes that AI generates sustainable value only when technological capability is matched by organisational readiness, responsible governance, effective human–AI collaboration and continuous workforce development. The discussion elaborates the implications of the model for strategic decision-making, operations, marketing, human resource management and finance, and considers the ethical, social and implementation challenges that accompany adoption. The paper contributes a theoretically grounded and integrative framework that can guide future empirical research and support managers who seek to adopt AI responsibly and effectively.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The green and digital transitions do not automatically produce inclusive growth. They interact through distinct labour-market processes: green structural change reallocates employment across sectors and places, whereas artificial intelligence (AI) reorganises tasks and authority within workplaces. This article develops a process-based conceptual framework for examining when their interaction can support AI-enabled green growth. An integrative review brings together peer-reviewed research and recent comparative reports. The framework follows a directional sequence in which green restructuring and AI deployment generate sectoral reallocation and task/workplace reorganisation. Labour-market adjustment arrangements and structural context then shape how these mechanisms lead to environmental, productivity, employment, job-quality, and distributive outcomes. These elements are not specified as independent, dependent, mediator, or moderator variables because the article does not estimate a statistical model. The framework distinguishes an enabling pathway based on labour augmentation and shared productivity gains from an adverse pathway involving displacement, surveillance, unequal value capture, and ecological externalisation. Six propositions identify relationships for subsequent empirical examination. A renewable-electricity value-chain application illustrates why AI exposure and labour effects differ across manufacturing, construction, and operations. The contribution is a power-sensitive account that treats environmental improvement and decent work as joint and institutionally contingent outcomes.Keywords: twin transition, artificial intelligence, labour-market adaptation, just transition, green growth.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Communication can feel intelligible, support competent action, or secure agreement while remaining poorly explained or unwarranted. This article introduces the Ubiquitous Sphoṭa–Pratibhā model to examine these divergences within situated meaning episodes. Comparative conceptual reconstruction brings Bhartṛhari’s linguistic wholeness and pratibhā into dialogue with communication theory, while distinguishing intrinsic reflexivity from reflective review. Sphoṭa and pratibhā identify structural and apprehensive perspectives on one episode of understanding, rather than successive processing stages. The model follows how apprehended import changes through formulation, public uptake and appraisal. It distinguishes experienced intelligibility, demonstrated grasp, articulation, coordination, warrant and fidelity to documented intention. A worked educational encounter shows how these achievements separate in human–AI communication. Four prospective propositions specify testable extensions and their possible failures. The contribution is an integrative architecture connecting lived understanding to public accountability; claims of additional predictive value remain open to comparison with cognitive and pragmatic alternatives.Keywords: communication theory; sphoṭa; pratibhā; consciousness; meaning; epistemic appraisal; human–AI communication

Abstract The "Provisional specification.pdf" introduces a comprehensive security architecture for governing autonomous artificial intelligence agents across isolated runtimes, administrative domains, and hardware environments. As AI agents increasingly invoke external tools and modify persistent data, the system distinguishes between an agent's ability to compute and its authority to execute consequential external effects. The architecture intercepts proposed agent operations, holding them in a non-effective state while a protected enforcement domain evaluates operation-specific authorization conditions and commits validation evidence. A scoped, non-bearer finality capability is then verified at an effectuation sink before the operation can produce real-world consequences. The specification covers advanced technical mechanisms including micro-virtual-machine isolation, task-preserving context minimization, distributed revocation, and hardware-level command accounting. Why You Should Download This Document You should download this specification if you are building, securing, or deploying autonomous AI agents that interact with enterprise resources, financial systems, or cloud infrastructure. It provides a detailed blueprint for preventing unauthorized external actions caused by prompt injection, compromised models, or hallucinated tool invocations. The document offers actionable implementations for deploying agents within virtual machines, micro-virtual machines, and OS-level containers while maintaining strict cryptographic and hardware-assisted oversight over API requests, network egress, and persistent memory mutations. Meta's newly launched Muse agent runs in isolated, secure virtual machines on the cloud to execute multi-step tasks across connected applications while attempting to limit unintended access to user credentials and ad systems. The specification provides a formalized, enterprise-grade extension of this concept, detailing how to implement micro-virtual-machine isolation and lifecycle-bound authority so that an agent's access to a tool connector does not automatically grant unrestricted execution rights. Similarly, as NVIDIA scales its AI hardware and NIM microservices for agentic workflows, the specification’s coverage of hardware-resident effect-budget accounting, accelerator-memory sanitization, and hardware queue containment offers a precise technical framework for securing agent workloads at the GPU and DPU layer

Volcanism should be understood as planetary infrastructure: a means by which internal activity supplies and renews surface environments, as well as a source of acute hazard. This paper argues that explaining Earth's long-term habitability requires placing volcanic processes within a coupled interior–surface system. Geological carbon cycling supplies the strongest mechanism, while stagnant-lid models, Venus, and the Lost City ecosystem distinguish supported mechanisms from universal necessity claims. The framework organizes the argument around supply, transformation, removal, and response time. This is a selective synthesis of published literature; it reports no new measurements, simulations, or independent model replications. Version 1.0 corrects and substantially revises the earlier web essay, including its claims about subduction, volatile delivery, extinction causation, and direct access to magma. documents.abstract: This article analyzes the current organization of counterintelligence in the United States. In today’s evolving security environment, characterized by globalization and multidimensional threats, counterintelligence has become a vital tool for protecting fundamental state interests. Ukraine is currently fighting a war against Russia while simultaneously standing at the center of a global geopolitical confrontation. Therefore, studying the American counterintelligence model and adopting its best practices is crucial for strengthening Ukraine’s national security. The study highlights that the United States lacks both a single consolidated law governing counterintelligence and a unified agency to conduct it. Instead, the American model is highly diversified and extraterritorial. The Director of National Intelligence coordinates these efforts under the guidance of the US President. Particular attention is given to the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency, which plays a pivotal role in ensuring personnel, industrial, and technological security. A significant portion of the research analyzes the current US National Counterintelligence Strategy (2024–2027), noting a substantial expansion of what requires counterintelligence protection. Beyond traditional government institutions, US counterintelligence now focuses on safeguarding advanced technologies, the national innovation base, large datasets, and critical supply chains. Furthermore, it actively protects the integrity of society and democratic institutions against the threat of informational influence campaigns. Based on the study’s findings, the author has formulated 16 initiatives to improve the effectiveness of Ukraine’s counterintelligence. It is proposed to expand the goals and objectives of counterintelligence and to adopt a Counterintelligence Strategy for Ukraine. It is recommended that the Security Service of Ukraine should be assigned additional counterintelligence functions related to the protection of domestic cutting-edge technologies and innovations, as well as supply chains; the assessment of the reliability of private companies fulfilling defense contracts; monitoring individuals with security clearances; and annually informing the public about the status and trends in threats to Ukraine’s national interests in the field of state security. Furthermore, the author suggests delineating offensive and defensive counterintelligence measures at the legislative level. It is also necessary to regulate the use of artificial intelligence in this field and strengthen the institutional capacity of prosecutors to oversee the legal compliance of domestic intelligence agencies. Finally, to safeguard human rights and freedoms, the article advocates for establishing robust parliamentary oversight by creating the position of a Special Representative of the Ukrainian Ombudsman.

Visual impairment restricts independent mobility and exposes people to collisions, falls and unsafe road situations. White canes and guide dogs remain the main aids, but they give little information about what an obstacle is, how far away it is, or when the user needs help. Artificial intelligence (AI) combined with wearable sensing and the Internet of Things (IoT) is increasingly proposed as a route to smart navigation and safety systems that perceive the scene, guide the user by audio or touch, and alert caregivers in an emergency. This paper presents a focused narrative review of five verified studies, published between 2018 and 2026 in IEEE, MDPI and River Publishers outlets, that cover sensor-based safety alerting, RGB-D and deep-learning navigation, machine-learning smart cane and glasses, edge-TPU indoor navigation, and an AIoT eyewear system with LiDAR ranging and an SOS function. The review examines sensing, AI perception, feedback and IoT integration. The literature shows that recent systems report object-detection accuracy of about 95 % and centimetre-level distance error in controlled tests, and that low-cost edge hardware such as the Raspberry Pi with a Google Coral TPU can run navigation models on the wearable itself. However, evidence is dominated by small prototypes, controlled or indoor settings, heterogeneous metrics and limited testing with visually impaired users, and few systems join navigation, perception and caregiver-facing safety in one design. The paper contributes a comparative analysis of the studies, a proposed conceptual “Third Eye” architecture that links wearable sensing, edge AI, IoT safety alerts and field validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and directions.

documents.abstract: This thesis analyzes modern technological solutions and mathematical models for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into organizational management systems. The study focuses on predictive analytics, Robotic Process Automation (RPA), HR analytics, and multi-agent decision support frameworks. The main objective of the research is to enhance operational efficiency, minimize human-factor errors, optimize resource allocation, and establish a data-driven strategic management architecture.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support decision-making, automate tasks, personalize services, and improve system performance across domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and workplace productivity. As AI adoption expands, clearer guidance is needed to connect human-centered design principles with measurable human outcomes. This systematic review synthesized 44 empirical studies on human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) to examine measurement approaches, framework categories, AI roles, and domain-specific findings. The reviewed studies showed that AI support was often associated with improved objective outcomes, including task performance and decision quality. Subjective outcomes, including trust, satisfaction, usability, workload, and perceived control, were more variable and depended on transparency, explanation design, task fit, user expertise, and the level of human control. Across studies, human-led AI support was the most common role, especially in high-stakes domains where humans retained final authority. Collaborative AI appeared in tasks requiring shared activity, feedback, or adaptive support, while AI-led support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems. Domain-specific findings showed that healthcare emphasized accuracy, reliability, and overreliance; education emphasized engagement, scaffolding, and ownership; transportation emphasized safety, timing, modality, and trust calibration; and other domains emphasized fairness, transparency, adoption, and acceptance. This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis that connects HCAI and HAX principles with AI roles, evaluation measures, and human outcomes, supporting future frameworks that are easier to evaluate and apply in real-world settings.

With artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly influencing children’s and youth’s lives, AI literacy has been promoted as an educational concern at all levels of schooling. While AI literacy initiatives are being introduced globally, the specific components and the objectives of this literacy remain undecided. This position paper challenges the current discourse of AI literacy by drawing attention to multiple purposes of AI literacy in middle school education that may co-exist and collide. We do so by applying Biesta’s world-centred education framework as an analytical lens, and by grounding the argument in classroom observations and interviews with middle school students. Our findings highlight both tensions and overlaps between middle school students’ often vague and fragmented formal knowledge and skills (qualification) of what AI is and how it works, and their more developed reflections related to norms and ethical concerns (socialisation), as well as agency (subjectification). We suggest that for AI literacy to truly empower students, both curriculum design and professional development must account for a broad spectrum of educational goals.

ToxPipe is a modular, fully open-source software stack designed to accelerate toxicological data analysis and decision-making by integrating large language model (LLM) capabilities with workflow, monitoring, and user-interface services. ToxPipe leverages existing open-source technologies like LibreChat, LiteLLM, and Langflow to provide centralized and streamlined access to different LLMs for end users and developers and logging and auditing of LLM use for organizations. ToxPipe also allows for open-source/local model support. While the ToxPipe ecosystem also supports advanced AI functions such as MCP server integration, RAG and literature search, and agent creation, we did not observe clear benefits using these configurations relative to the GPT-5.5 baseline assertion coverage scores. ToxPipe is available as a series of Docker containers for rapid and reproducible deployment.

documents.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) in sub-8-bit arithmetic promises substantial gains in memory bandwidth and compute throughput, yet FP4 formats introduce quantization error severe enough to destabilize optimization if left unaddressed. We present ALTO, an open-source training recipe for GPT-OSS-20B, a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, on the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark under the MXFP4 microscaling format. The recipe combines established techniques from Abecassis, Felix et al. [arXiv:2509.25149] (hybrid 1D/2D block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, and stochastic rounding) with a simplified weight de-oscillation scheme adapted from TetraJet-v2 [arXiv:2510.27527]. On C4 validation at global batch size 16, MXFP4 + RHT + SR + de-oscillation reaches a validation loss of 3.3350 at 16,128 steps, only 0.007 above the BF16 baseline (3.3283), closing roughly 50% of the gap left by MXFP4 without de-oscillation (3.3418). Measured by steps to reach the MLPerf quality target (validation loss 3.34), de-oscillation cuts the FP4 convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0%. We also report negative end-to-end results from differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling, despite each showing operator-level SNR gains. All experiments use simulated MXFP4 kernels on AMD MI300 hardware and wall-clock speed has not been optimized.

The modern democratic state is characterised by a structural anomaly that has long confounded political sociology and institutional theory: populations of advanced, highly complex societies live under the continuous, dense administration of unelected specialists, yet they periodically delegate supreme formal authority to a single individual selected on the basis of campaign performance and diffuse public trust. Max Weber diagnosed this condition, recognising the permanent, rationalised bureaucracy as the most efficient and indestructible organisational form in human history, while warning of its tendency to become an "iron cage" devoid of ultimate values. To prevent this, he prescribed the charismatic leader, empowered by plebiscitary democracy, who would supply the state with ends and hold the experts in check. This article argues, following Berkovski (2026), that the remedy is itself a paradox: the more specialised the administrative machine, the more the leader depends on the bureaucracy's monopoly over knowledge. Berkovski's Oakeshottian alternative — officialdom checked by rival officialdom — is sound but remains analog, slow and exposed to ossification, capture and the Schmittian critique of liberal parliamentarianism. Drawing on polycentric governance, agile public administration and agentic artificial intelligence, the article proposes a framework of fluid institutions organised on Adaptive, Agentic and Agile (AAA) principles. It maps Ostrom's eight design principles onto algorithmic governance, confronts the documented failures of automated administration, and concludes that the structural permanence of bureaucracy is no longer an insurmountable precondition of state capacity, provided that files are kept open, algorithms auditable and human accountability intact. Subtitle: Knowledge monopolies, plural checking and the Adaptive, Agentic and Agile state. Companion to the anatomical review of Berkovski (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23577500).

The intersection of AI and digital forensics symbolizes the paradigm shift in criminal investigation and protection against cybercrimes. The chapter discusses the ways in which AI technologies will radically change the process of forensic practices, making it faster, more accurate, and comprehensive when analyzing digital evidence. The combination of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision with the forensic workflow has created unprecedented opportunities regarding the processing of large amounts of digital data, detecting intricate trends, and automating formerly labor-intensive aspects of the investigation process. Modern forensic investigations are witnessing a geometric increase in the volumes of data available to them, in multiple forms such as IoT-based devices, social media platforms, encrypted communications, and advanced vectors of cyberattacks. The intelligent automation, predictive analytics, and adaptive learning mechanisms are AI-based solutions to these problems. Nevertheless, this technological development presents urgent concerns about interpretability, bias, privacy, and admissibility in court. The chapter discusses the theoretical background, its practical use, transformative advantages, and ongoing issues, as well as the future directions of AI-enabled digital forensics, in a thorough analysis of how intelligent systems are changing the face of forensic science and criminal justice.

This study examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to support early childhood education (ECE) in addressing workforce pressures, inequality, and quality-related challenges, while identifying the organisational, pedagogical, and ethical conditions required for responsible AI use. An interpretivist qualitative design was used with 22 participants (8 head teachers and 14 early childhood teachers) from ECE institutions in Sydney, Australia, who took part in semi-structured face-to-face interviews. Six interconnected themes emerged from inductive thematic analysis: workforce and operational challenges; AI awareness and readiness; AI as teacher support, not replacement; AI and equity; AI and learning quality; and responsible AI adoption. Participants considered how AI could support planning, documentation, translation, administration, and personalised learning, freeing up time for meaningful teacher–child interaction. They stressed, however, that AI cannot address structural workforce shortages and cannot take the place of teachers’ relational, professional, and safeguarding roles. The study’s contribution lies in bringing together workforce, equity, learn-ing quality, and responsible AI adoption within a single ECE-focused empirical framework, and in highlighting the necessity of human-centred implementation. Longitudinal and mixed-methods studies in various settings are needed to inves-tigate the impact of AI on teacher workload, child outcomes, equity, and policy implementation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the global travel and tourism industry is reshaping workforce competency requirements. This chapter examines the growing need for reskilling and upskilling in AI-enabled travel environments. Drawing on human capital theory, technology acceptance frameworks, and organizational learning models, it identifies skills displaced by automation and highlights emerging competencies that complement AI. A taxonomy of AI-related and human-centered capabilities required for sustainable employment in travel and tourism is proposed. The chapter also evaluates corporate training initiatives, public–private partnerships, and government-led workforce development strategies. Particular attention is given to equity concerns affecting frontline and low-wage workers, with recommendations for inclusive skill-development pathways. The chapter concludes with practical and policy recommendations for educators, employers, and policymakers, along with directions for future research.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly integrating into mental health and wellness spaces, yet many tools are developed in silos, lacking essential clinical and ethical guidance. This chapter provides a critical bridge, positioning the art therapist as a co-leader and essential “Human-in-the-Loop” for GenAI development. It begins with a comprehensive literature review on GenAI applications, benefits, and ethical challenges in the mental health and wellness spaces. The core of the chapter is a human-centered design case study that serves as a blueprint for interdisciplinary collaboration, demonstrating how lived-experience and clinical insight form the requirements for technology developers. Finally, an innovative Exploratory Exercise shows art therapists how to translate their intuitive therapeutic directives into a technical design brief, clearly separating the AI’s procedural support role (e.g., generating reflective prompts) from the therapist’s irreplaceable relational role (empathy and validation). This framework ensures new mental health technology is grounded in therapeutic wisdom, promoting safe, trustworthy, and human-centered innovation.

Justification: Deficiencies in proportional reasoning with which students enter higher education affect the understanding of more complex content; therefore, pedagogical strategies are required to help overcome these difficulties. Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of artificial intelligence–based tutoring in strengthening proportional reasoning among first-semester students at a public university in the province of Manabí, Ecuador. Methodology: A quantitative approach with a descriptive-comparative scope was adopted, using a pre-experimental pretest–posttest design with two groups. The sample consisted of 78 students. The intervention involved tutoring supported by artificial intelligence tools, structured in two stages: prior knowledge construction and proportional problem solving. Data were collected using two performance tests designed to assess the identification, structuring, and application of proportional relationships. Results: After the pedagogical intervention, the results showed a shift toward higher performance levels in both groups, with a reduction in the low level and a significant increase in the high level. Specifically, improvements were observed in the identification, structuring, and application of proportional relationships; however, the change in identification was less pronounced. Inferential analyses revealed statistically significant differences between the pretest and posttest (p < .001), with large effect sizes. Conclusion: Artificial intelligence–based tutoring strengthened proportional reasoning among the first-semester students who participated in this study.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Supervising a multi-UAV reconnaissance mission usually means plotting waypoints and watching every drone. We present UAV SwarmAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system in which an operator states the mission in one natural-language sentence and a ground-station agent writes and executes code that turns it into per-UAV routes. The agent grounds inspection targets in an aerial map with a vision-language model, splits them among N UAVs by balancing route length, and dispatches worker agents that verify incidents with a compact onboard decision model. In simulation over 4 incident types and 3 foundation models, the swarm located the incident in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%). A paired scaling study with one to 5 UAVs shows that flight time follows an Amdahl-type law. The second UAV delivers half of the attainable saving and the speedup is bounded at 1.52x. We discuss what this predictability, and the false alarms we observed, imply for an operator who supervises the swarm, and outline the user study needed to test it.

Objective: To analyze the digital behavior of university students at the State University of Montes Claros (Unimontes), considering their use of electronic devices, visual hygiene and ergonomic habits, ocular symptoms, and associated biopsychosocial aspects. Methods: A cross-sectional, descriptive, quantitative study was conducted between August and November 2025, involving 154 students enrolled in Medicine and Mathematics programs at Unimontes. Data were collected using a structured online questionnaire comprising 28 questions on sociodemographic characteristics, digital exposure, ergonomic habits, and ocular symptoms. Descriptive analysis was performed using absolute and relative frequencies. Results: The mean age was 25.45 years (SD = 5.75), with a predominance of female participants (55.2%). All participants used digital devices for academic purposes, with a mean daily exposure of 4.97 hours for studying and 3.63 hours for leisure. Laptops were the most frequently used devices (81.2%), followed by smartphones (60.4%). Regarding ergonomics, 35.7% did not take breaks. Mean sleep duration was 6.45 hours, and 62.4% considered their sleep quality inadequate. Only one participant (0.6%) reported no ocular symptoms. The most frequent symptoms were eye fatigue (48.7%), screen-related headaches (45.5%), and dry eyes (33.8%). Shoulder or neck pain was reported by 44.2% of participants. Conclusion: High levels of screen exposure were observed, alongside inadequate ergonomic habits, unsatisfactory sleep, and a high frequency of ocular symptoms. These findings highlight the need for educational interventions in academic settings to promote healthy digital device use.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the global travel industry by enhancing service delivery, operational efficiency, and customer engagement. However, successful AI adoption depends not only on technological capabilities but also on organizational culture. This chapter examines the relationship between organizational culture and AI readiness across travel-sector organizations, including airlines, hotels, online travel agencies, and destination management organizations. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Competing Values Framework (CVF), and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, it explores how cultural dimensions such as leadership orientation, innovation climate, knowledge sharing, and adaptability to change influence AI adoption. The chapter highlights key barriers and enablers of AI readiness, offers practical strategies for fostering an AI-ready culture, and discusses managerial implications and future research directions.

Purpose This study aims to examine the determinants of student satisfaction with their experience of using artificial intelligence (AI) tools for learning-related activities in Vietnamese higher education, addressing a gap in research that has focused primarily on AI adoption and usage, with limited evidence on students’ post-use satisfaction in an emerging-market higher education context. Design/methodology/approach A construct-level framework informed by selected insights from the technology acceptance model (TAM) and self-determination theory (SDT) was used to organise perceived credibility, content quality, perceived utility, cognitive absorption and emotional wellbeing within one explanatory model. Survey data from 380 undergraduate business students were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Findings All five factors were positively associated with satisfaction. The findings indicate that students’ satisfaction depends not only on the functional value of generative AI tools but also on the credibility of their outputs and the cognitive and emotional quality of the learning experience. Originality/value This study shifts attention from AI adoption to satisfaction as a post-use evaluative outcome. Rather than testing TAM or SDT in their entirety, it uses selected insights from both theories to organise complementary technology-related and experiential determinants within a single construct-level framework.

Purpose As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life and workplace operations, research has begun to document numerous organizational benefits, including enhanced efficiency and productivity. However, employees’ personal experiences with AI and how these experiences spill over into the work domain remain underexplored. Using sociomateriality as a sensitizing lens, we propose and test a sequential process in which personal AI use increases work-related AI use, further enhancing employees’ psychological capital, ultimately improving their service innovation performance. We further examine conscientiousness as an important boundary condition that moderates this pathway. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 uses a three-wave survey of 438 service employees and employs structural equation modeling to test the hypothesized serial mediation. Study 2 extends this investigation by examining within-person dynamics using a daily experience sampling design with 121 participants and testing the moderating role of conscientiousness. Findings Across both studies, personal AI use positively predicts employees’ work-related AI use, which in turn increases their psychological capital and subsequently service innovation performance. Moreover, employees lower in conscientiousness benefit more from AI use. Originality/value This paper contributes to our understanding of personal AI use’s spillover effect in the work domain, suggesting AI use may introduce psychological affordances that were less evident in earlier technologies. Our research demonstrates that individual personality differences can influence the effectiveness of human–AI collaboration.

Agribusiness supply chains are exposed to climate variability, biological uncertainty, perishability, demand volatility, infrastructure constraints, and fragmented coordination among farmers, processors, traders, logistics providers, retailers, and regulators. These vulnerabilities increasingly intersect with the transition toward lower-carbon production and distribution. Artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) offer complementary capabilities: connected sensors and devices can capture field, storage, processing, and transport conditions, while AI can convert heterogeneous data into forecasts, anomaly alerts, and operational recommendations. This article examines how AI–IoT integration can improve supply chain resilience and operational efficiency while supporting carbon-neutrality transitions in agribusiness. An integrative review of recent academic research and authoritative reports is used to develop a theory-informed framework. The synthesis identifies six pathways: end-to-end visibility, predictive risk sensing, adaptive planning, quality and loss control, low-carbon operational optimization, and collaborative learning. It also identifies important boundary conditions, including data quality, connectivity, interoperability, managerial capabilities, farmer participation, cybersecurity, financing, and governance. The analysis cautions that digital adoption does not automatically create resilience or sustainability: poorly designed systems can intensify dependence on vendors, exclude smallholders, optimize local efficiency at the expense of system-wide performance, or increase energy use without reducing absolute emissions. The article proposes a phased implementation model and research propositions linking AI IoT capability to resilience, efficiency, and environmental outcomes. It argues that the strategic value of smart agribusiness should be assessed through verified reductions in disruption exposure, avoidable losses, resource intensity, and emissions—not through technology deployment alone.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems become more capable, their behavior may become increasingly difficult to predict. This article examines whether behavioral unpredictability necessarily undermines the ability to govern consequential AI actions. It argues that uncertainty about what a system may propose does not, by itself, defeat action-specific pre-execution authorization. The analysis distinguishes three separate properties: predicting a system's behavior, determining whether a proposed action is permitted under applicable policy and authority, and enforcing that determination before execution. It challenges the assumption that assigning a second, equally or more intelligent AI system to supervise the first resolves the governance problem. Collusion, common-mode failures, and recursive supervision raise questions that additional intelligence alone cannot settle. It separates standing eligibility from runtime authorization: a test-then-trust regime releases on a prior assessment and is exactly as vulnerable to concealed capability as its critics say, while action-specific authorization gates each consequential action under the policy in force at execution. And it distinguishes the authorization requirement, which does not change as capability grows, from the deployment-specific evidence that a boundary remains complete and independent, which must remain valid under the capability model actually in scope. The article develops a three-part analytical framework distinguishing evaluation independence, authority independence, and enforcement independence. It explains why independently derived evaluations do not automatically confer permission, why intelligent supervisors may exercise legitimately delegated authority without becoming an alternative execution path, and why consequential release must remain dependent on an independently enforced authorization verdict. The central architectural argument is conditional. Enforceable authorization requires demonstrated coverage of governed effect-bearing execution paths, protection of the enforcement mechanism against unauthorized control, adequate governing inputs, and valid authority. A boundary-emitted ALLOW permits release; DENY and unresolved ABSTAIN prevent execution. A tamper-evident authorization artifact supports independent reconstruction of the verdict, while separate execution-path evidence is needed to establish that release actually depended on that verdict. The article also examines the limits of this approach, including compromised supervisory determinations, defective authorization inputs, improperly established policy authority, unauthorized AI proliferation outside governed environments, and harmful outcomes from legitimately authorized actions. It does not claim that authorization guarantees safe behavior or universal AI containment. Central conclusion: Behavioral unpredictability does not remove the requirement for enforceable permission over consequential actions. Unpredictability is not permission. Scope A doctrine article in the FERZ AI Governance Corpus. Its claims are analytical and conditional; it asserts no implementation-specific capability and describes no FERZ product. The canonical publication is the ferz.ai page: ferz.ai/articles/unpredictable-intelligence-still-requires-authorization. This record is the citable version of record for the edition. topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This mixed-methods systematic review examines the evidence for the safe integration of large language model (LLM)-based mental health support into university counseling services, and the policy, ethical, and governance frameworks that shape that integration. The review is guided by a convergent segregated design (Hong et al., 2018) and reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021) and ENTREQ (Tong et al., 2012). Four theoretical perspectives structure the review: the RE-AIM framework for implementation science (Glasgow et al., 1999), biomedical ethics (Beauchamp & Childress, 2019), AI governance (Floridi et al., 2018; Novelli et al., 2024), and an integrated model of LLM-mediated mental health support, with cultural responsiveness as a cross-cutting dimension. A four-block Boolean search was executed across EBSCOhost, ProQuest, PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore (plus Cochrane CENTRAL), yielding 2,172 records; after filtering, 365 topic-relevant records were screened, 151 unique records were identified, and 138 full texts were retrieved for deep text screening. Data are extracted across twelve domains covering study and intervention characteristics, quantitative and safety outcomes, therapeutic alliance, RE-AIM implementation dimensions, policy and governance, qualitative findings, MMAT 2018 quality appraisal, and meta-analysis data. A random-effects meta-analysis was pre-specified for any outcome domain with at least three comparable studies; following data extraction, this was not feasible because fewer than three studies per outcome domain reported between-group effect sizes in a common metric, means and standard deviations were frequently unreported, and pre-post correlations were not reported in any study. Quantitative synthesis therefore proceeds as a structured narrative synthesis (Popay et al., 2006; McKenzie & Brennan, 2021) with direction-of-effect coding, thematic synthesis of qualitative findings using a 40-theme framework, and a narrative policy and governance synthesis, integrated at the interpretation stage across the RE-AIM dimensions. GRADE is applied at the outcome level using a structured narrative approach (Murad et al., 2017).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract River sand mining represents a direct and intensive form of human intervention into the sediment flow system. Unlike dams or bank protection works that mainly modify flow conditions, sand mining extracts the physical material that maintains channel stability, disturbing sediment balance and causing long-term riverbed lowering and bank erosion. In large basins, the problem becomes more serious when sediment supply is already reduced by upstream hydropower dams. The combined effect often creates sediment deficits, increasing the risk of channel instability and downstream impacts. This study presents a systematic synthesis of research published between 1995 and 2025, integrating existing approaches into three main methodological groups: (i) longterm statistical analysis, (ii) remote sensing combined with artificial intelligence for large-scale monitoring, and (iii) hydrodynamic-morphological modeling for process-based assessment. This study advances a mechanistic perspective that explicitly links sediment deficit to morpho-dynamic responses across spatial scales, from local scour development to basin-wide channel adjustment and delta degradation. A novel sediment balance-based framework is proposed that connects monitoring systems, system resilience, sediment dynamics, and management decisions within a unified causal structure. Unlike existing frameworks that are primarily descriptive or policyoriented, the proposed framework emphasizes process-based linkages between human interventions and river responses, providing a more explicit basis for risk assessment and adaptive management of sand mining activities. This work contributes to shifting river resource management from extraction-based approaches toward sediment balance-oriented strategies for sustainable river system governance.

Abstract Functional MRI (fMRI) has traditionally focused on grey matter activations, overlooking the contribution of white matter pathways to brain organisation. Yet evidence suggests that white matter constrains, modulates, and integrates signals across distant regions. Here, we introduce a framework to map the functional specialisation of white matter circuits using fMRI scans collected while participants watched naturalistic videos. By leveraging ecologically valid stimuli, this method captures cognition as it naturally unfolds. Integrating fMRI with brain connections, we derived a functionally grounded parcellation of the connectome, challenging conventional cortical-based cognitive taxonomy. Distinct cognitive profiles emerged for association and commissural fibres, with association pathways preferentially linked to language-related processes and commissural pathways to executive and motor functions, affirming the functionally heterogeneous nature of white matter systems. An artificial intelligence framework applied to independent datasets confirmed the robustness and functional relevance of the identified parcels. This open-access framework also enables the interactive exploration of white matter functional organisation, offering a new lens on the neural bases of cognition.

The demand for better training dataset to enhance the reliability of the models has increased due to the fast. In the case of deep-learning-based developments in AI. But what may be problematic is the task of large dataset gathering and maintenance. There are several challenges, especially in areas where information is confidential own or limited available. One such generative AI is the approach that has offered the answers to the problems concerning privacy. It helps in generating synthetic data for training intents with the use of AI models. It is designed to present a extensive overview of generative AI techniques and their application of VAEs and GANs for producing synthetic data. Prior to that, we also talked about earlier studies in the field, critically examined these generative issues, biases, and organizational validation processes, and offered models for their efficacy using synthetic data. In this study we have reflected that generative AI might be able to develop models that perform well by creating synthetic data like real-world data. This research shows how generative AI can revolutionize many industries by its private and low-cost method of producing training data. This research will affect future developments and applications in the development of AI with the help of generative AI.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to manage bycatch and discards is a growing interest in fisheries. However, implementing AI in fisheries faces challenges despite its promised benefits. This study evaluates the applications, challenges, and opportunities of adopting AI to reduce bycatch and discards using the Technology-Organization-External business environment (TOE) framework. We reviewed literature to identify projects using AI to manage bycatch and discards, conducted 17 in-depth interviews with fishery stakeholders, and supplemented these insights by attending two fishery innovation-related events. We identified several use cases of AI in managing bycatch and discards, including real-time species identification during fishing and catch registration, on-board automated sorting of species via conveyor belt and robotics, integration of AI with smart fishing gear, environmental-DNA sampling, and data-driven decision making in fishing. Several challenges hinder the adoption of AI-based tools in fisheries. First, most use-cases are at developmental, pilot, or prototype stage, suggesting the technology is not yet fully mature. Second, there is limited acceptance of AI-based tools among fishers due to concerns about trust, privacy, security, lack of incentives, and human replacement. Third, the need for high-quality big data and the complexity of modelling ecological systems make AI-models questionable. This study highlights three recommendations: (1) cross-sector collaboration to promote trust, support science-based policies and decisions, and make AI-based tools more feasible for fishers; (2) combining economic instruments on bycatch and discards with AI adoption to make it more attractive to fishers; and (3) using data management technologies to create trust in sharing data.

This article examines the didactic potential, methodological foundations, and practical challenges of using artificial intelligence in English language teaching. It discusses generative AI, intelligent chatbots, automated writing feedback systems, speech recognition technologies, and adaptive learning platforms as tools for developing learners’ communicative competence.

This chapter explains how PhD students can use large language models (LLMs) to support research without outsourcing scholarship. It covers practical uses in writing, literature exploration, coding, experiment planning, and self-critique, while emphasizing that you remain responsible for accuracy, reasoning, and originality. The chapter highlights common failure modes such as fabricated citations, confident errors, and overly agreeable “reviews,” and discusses when LLM feedback is helpful versus misleading. It also outlines responsible use, including disclosure norms, bias awareness, and protecting confidential data. The goal is to benefit from speed and breadth while staying intellectually in control.

Implicit surfaces are widely used in computer modeling due to their ability to model complex objects with relatively little data. Also, in contrast with explicit ways of modelling, such as with triangle meshes and boundary representation of parametric surfaces, the implicit surfaces are guaranteed to keep continuity and smoothness under the operations of deformation or replication. The explicit modeling, however, such as triangle mesh or boundary representation of parametric surfaces, is the de facto current standard of computer modeling. The problem of conversion from the explicit representation to an implicit one is therefore a cutting-edge engineering problem. New approaches and specific methods are published every year, including those that are based on machine learning or artificial intelligence in general. In this work, we explore the limits of a triangle mesh to implicit surface conversion based on Fourier polynomial approximation, although the polynomial we propose contains fractional terms. The prospects of using a polynomial with solely integer terms are limited by the Fourier polynomial`s tendency to overfit. We show that adding fractional terms to the integer ones in a single function allows for reaching the modeling quality that could be satisfactory for some practical scenarios, while keeping the total amount of polynomial coefficients relatively small too. In theory, using the Fourier polynomial with fractional terms could be used not only for smooth surface modeling but for smooth connection of different triply periodic surfaces along a selected plane due to the planned loss of periodicity along the normal axis. This, however, requires studying the question of specific per-axis polynomial configuration, which extends beyond the scope of this particular paper.

Background/Objectives: Image-based wound assessment may vary among experienced nurses. This study examined inter-nurse variability and concordance with three multimodal generative artificial intelligence models. Methods: In this exploratory cross-sectional comparative study, 18 nurses with wound-care expertise and ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude independently assessed 30 de-identified wound images from León, Spain, across seven assessment and treatment-related domains. Inter-nurse agreement was summarized using modal shares and Gwet’s AC1. Concordance with the nurse modal set required an exact match with any response in the nurse modal set. Overall confidence intervals were estimated by case-clustered bootstrap resampling. No independent clinical reference standard was established. Results: The analyses quantified inter-nurse agreement and model concordance with the nurse modal set, not diagnostic accuracy. Inter-nurse agreement was highest for wound etiology (mean modal share, 71.3%; AC1, 0.520) and lowest for primary dressing selection (43.7%; AC1, 0.163). Overall concordance was 63.3% (95% confidence interval, 56.7–70.0) for Gemini, 48.6% (40.5–56.2) for ChatGPT, and 44.8% (38.6–51.4) for Claude. Gemini exceeded ChatGPT by 14.8 percentage points and Claude by 18.6 percentage points in exploratory comparisons of overall concordance with the nurse modal set. Complete intermodel agreement occurred in 38.6% of 210 case–domain tasks. Conclusions: Image-based wound assessments varied among experienced nurses, and model concordance with the nurse modal set differed across assessment domains and evaluated systems. Concordance with the nurse modal set reflects agreement with the panel’s most frequently selected responses. It does not establish clinical correctness, clinical validity, or an ability to resolve clinical ambiguity: image-only assessment, the small purposive sample, and reliance on a nurse-derived comparator limit interpretation. Further validation in clinical contexts and against independent reference standards is needed before these models can support wound-care decisions.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Hand landmarks serve as input for gesture recognition, sign language understanding, and touchless human-computer interaction. Yet hand pose estimators are typically evaluated with frame-wise localization metrics such as PCK or MPJPE, which are computed over matched predictions and overlook missed or spurious hands, handedness errors, and temporal instability. To address these limitations, we present VERA-Hand, a benchmark that evaluates estimators using manually verified, frame-level 2D annotations for 10,690 hands across four complementary dimensions (detection, localization, identification, and temporal stability), as well as a joint Pose-F1 metric that requires both correct detection and accurate localization. Evaluating six estimators spanning hand-specific, whole-body, reconstruction-based, and foundation-model paradigms, we find that no estimator dominates: rankings reorder sharply across dimensions. VERA-Hand also exposes failures that localization-only and downstream evaluations may not reveal, including cross-hand overlap in over 85% of frames for a recent foundation model. A post-hoc cleanup case study demonstrates how the benchmark can validate corrective interventions, while stratified analyses show that robustness varies across motion-blur classes and hand regions. We release the verified annotations, protocol, and code at https://gibranbenitez.github.io/VERA_Hand/

topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Surgical outcomes depend on operative precision, making instrument tracking essential for assessing surgeon performance. Sensor and marker-based approaches raise sterilization and ergonomic concerns, whereas vision-based markerless approaches enable tracking directly from surgical videos. However, markerless instrument tracking has predominantly focused on minimally invasive surgery, where video capture is inherently available, unlike in open surgery. Comprehensive reviews on markerless instrument tracking in open surgery, particularly motion tracking and pose estimation beyond conventional 2D analyses, are lacking. To address this gap, we present a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, searching five databases (PubMed, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and ACM Digital Library) for studies reporting markerless tool motion tracking or pose estimation during open surgery. Of 2084 articles screened, 14 were included in the review. Deep learning (DL) was used in 12 studies, while classical computer vision (CV) and hybrid DL-CV approaches were used in one study each. Outputs included pose estimation (n=8) and motion tracking (n=6). Orthopedic surgery using cadaver models was commonly reported (n=4), while skill assessment and infrastructure development/benchmarking were the most frequent applications (n=6 each). Surgical drills were the most tracked instruments (n=6), with majority of the articles utilizing simulated datasets (n=10). Most algorithms, among the 14 articles, relied on frame-wise estimation, suggesting that temporal dynamics may be underutilized. Overall, markerless tool tracking in open surgery remains at an early stage, with studies focusing largely on low-fidelity phantoms and cadaveric models. Further research is needed to improve robustness and applicability for real surgeries.

Private healthcare providers in India increasingly use image-driven social media platforms to communicate clinical services, promote health screenings, and establish institutional standing. This study examines visual health communication practices across four major private hospital networks in India: Apollo Hospitals, Manipal Hospitals, Medicover Hospitals, and Narayana Health. Informed by visual social semiotics and the Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM), a visual content analysis was conducted on 400 static Instagram posts (100 per network). The analysis investigated predominant health topics, design elements, persuasive rhetorical appeals, and visual framing strategies. Chi-square tests showed that the networks differed clearly in rhetorical appeals and only modestly in visual modality, but not in health topics or framing. The findings show that oncology (28.5%) and cardiovascular-metabolic conditions (23.2%) dominate the clinical agenda, consistent with India’s epidemiological transition toward non-communicable diseases. Visually, hospitals rely on 3D anatomical computer-generated imagery, metaphorical analogies (such as broken chalk representing sarcoma or decaying fruit representing viral hepatitis), and skeuomorphic smartphone user-interface elements. Rhetorical appeals emphasize institutional authority (ethos) through accreditation seals, academic accolades, and state-level inaugurations, balanced with emotional pediatric recovery narratives (pathos). Loss framing took the form of financial metaphors, such as a billing ledger of delayed care. In qualitative reading, Manipal and Apollo present artificial intelligence and robotics as markers of precision, whereas Narayana Health emphasizes accessible care pathways and patient costs, although framing did not differ significantly across networks. The results show how these hospitals handle public health education and patient acquisition within the same posts.

This paper explores State Religion Design (SSRD) as a hypothetical application domain of the Provenance-Suppression Model (PSM). The purpose is not to argue that any particular religion was designed by a state, nor that any existing historical tradition is the product of deliberate fabrication. Rather, the paper examines a systems-engineering problem: if a state desired to create, deploy, maintain, and transmit a religion across generations while concealing its authorship, what architectural, informational, and provenance-security requirements would be necessary?Building upon the Provenance-Suppression Model and the concept of Information Security Across Civilizational Timescales, the paper treats religion as a long-duration sociotechnical system capable of transmitting norms, identity, legitimacy, historical memory, and governance structures. Within this framework, religion becomes both an operational architecture and a potential information-security platform. The principal challenge is not system deployment but provenance protection. The resulting analysis demonstrates how concealment, epistemic conditions, and recovery barriers would function if the authorship of a religious system were itself considered a protected informational asset.

Improving the efficiency of GUI testing agents is important for industrial deployment. Beyond LLM inference, fixed waiting between consecutive interactions introduces substantial overhead. Our industrial study reveals that fixed waiting accounts for 42.3% of the time within the sampled interaction intervals, comparable to the 54.8% spent on model calls. Moreover, 62.9% of the waiting time is spent after the GUI has already finished loading. Although prior studies have proposed adaptive waiting strategies, their reliance on app-specific data or platform-specific information limits their applicability across diverse industrial environments. To this end, we propose WaitLens, which fine-tunes a lightweight VLM on GUI loading trajectories annotated with waiting end times. We introduce temporal resampling to construct diverse training examples, enabling the model to learn varying GUI loading behaviors from temporal observations. Experiments show that WaitLens achieves 86.08% accuracy in deciding whether to keep waiting, compared with 54.13% for the backbone VLM. Our evaluation using recordings from Meituan's industrial testing pipeline shows that WaitLens reduces mean extra waiting after the interface is ready by 94.98% compared with a 20-second fixed wait.

The increasing pressure on global freshwater resources has intensified the need for sustainable approaches in the planning, design, and operation of built environments. Interior spaces, although traditionally considered a minor contributor to environmental degradation compared with building structures, represent a significant opportunity for water conservation through efficient fixtures, intelligent monitoring systems, and integrated resource management strategies. Sustainable interior design has evolved beyond material selection and energy efficiency to incorporate advanced water management practices that minimize consumption, reduce wastewater generation, and enhance user awareness. Smart plumbing systems have emerged as a transformative approach by integrating Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensors, automated controls, real-time monitoring platforms, artificial intelligence (AI)-based analytics, and water-efficient technologies. These systems enable predictive maintenance, leak detection, adaptive water distribution, and optimized consumption patterns in residential, commercial, healthcare, and hospitality interiors. This review examines the relationship between water conservation principles and smart plumbing technologies within sustainable interior design projects. The study synthesizes recent research on low-flow fixtures, greywater recycling, rainwater integration, smart metering, sensor-based plumbing networks, and digital water management platforms. The review highlights that intelligent plumbing solutions can significantly reduce potable water demand while improving operational efficiency and occupant engagement. However, challenges including high initial investment, technological complexity, maintenance requirements, and limited integration between interior designers and building service engineers remain barriers to widespread adoption. Future research directions emphasize the development of affordable smart systems, data-driven water management frameworks, and interdisciplinary design approaches. The integration of sustainable interior design with intelligent plumbing infrastructure represents a critical pathway toward water-resilient and environmentally responsible buildings.

Context Animal welfare assessment on dairy farms increasingly combines resource-, management- and animal-based indicators to provide a comprehensive evaluation of farm conditions. However, information on the welfare performance of medium-sized dairy farms in Türkiye remains limited, particularly under regional production conditions. Aims This study aimed to assess the welfare performance of medium-sized dairy farms in Burdur Province, Türkiye, using management-, resource- and animal-based indicators; to identify the principal areas requiring improvement; and to explore associations among selected farm characteristics and welfare indicators. Methods This cross-sectional observational study included 91 voluntarily participating dairy farms with herd sizes ranging from 25 to 50 cattle in Burdur province, Türkiye. Data were collected during on-site farm visits using direct observations and structured questionnaires. Welfare assessment was evaluated using management-based indicators covering hygiene, health management, human factors and behavioural practices, together with animal-based indicators, including activity, cleanliness, faecal consistency and body condition score. A study-specific semi-quantitative management-based welfare score was calculated to summarise farm-level management performance. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, and associations between selected variables were examined using Spearman’s rank correlation analysis. Key results The mean management-based welfare score indicated generally low welfare performance across the surveyed farms. In the lowest domain, scores were recorded for human factors, hygiene and health management. Staff welfare training, quarantine and isolation practices, routine hoof care, and behavioural monitoring were uncommon. Animal-based indicators varied among farms, particularly in cleanliness and activity scores, whereas body condition and faecal consistency scores were generally within acceptable ranges. Conclusion This cross-sectional assessment provides a regional description of welfare performance in medium-sized dairy farms in Burdur Province, Türkiye. The findings identify staff training, hygiene, biosecurity, preventive health management, routine hoof care and behavioural monitoring as priority areas for farm-level improvement. The combined use of management-, resource- and animal-based indicators may support a more comprehensive assessment of dairy cattle welfare under regional production conditions. Implications The findings identify staff training, hygiene, biosecurity, preventive health management, routine hoof care and behavioural monitoring as practical priorities for regional farm-level welfare programs. Combining management-, resource- and animal-based indicators may support more comprehensive on-farm welfare assessment.

While multiple occupational health issues affect farm workers, evidence on the direct role of occupational therapy in addressing these is limited. Interventions could focus on ergonomic improvements, chemical exposure reduction, and mental health support to address these challenges.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Abstract Chapter 6 is the closing chapter of the book and concentrates on what comes next for imaginary companion research. The research presented earlier in the book is discussed and how it answers research questions but also brings up more for future studies. The chapter is laid out as two separate sections, one looking at phenomena akin to and how imaginary companions could fit into different interventions, and another looking at new research directions. The intervention section touches on the idea of creating an imaginary companion intervention that is socially prescribed. Social prescription is a way to link vulnerable populations to community support, so it would be a way to give the children who may not have the privilege of being able to imagine freely the chance to do so. Other intervention ideas that incorporate imaginary companions include the idea of Dungeons & Dragons, those with artificial intelligence and eye movement desensitization reprocessing therapy. The second section of the chapter looks at future directions in research. It suggests studies in pupillometry as one direction that hasn’t been explored. It also calls for more research on topics like the illusion of independent agency and private speech in reference to imaginary companion creation. There is a final suggestion that studies on what we have already found need to be replicated and that there are many studies to be run on things we do not know yet.

Abstract Editorial policies increasingly require authors to disclose substantive uses of generative AI, but such requirements commonly focus on whether, where, and how a model was used. Even function-specific disclosure may locate a model in the research or writing process without showing how its outputs entered scholarly judgment, how they were evaluated, or whether contributors can reconstruct the relevant reasoning and defend resulting claims without treating those outputs as sufficient justification. Drawing on research ethics, AI disclosure policy, human–model interaction, and researcher formation, this article argues that disclosure documents model use, whereas responsible use requires claim-level authorial warrant: a contributor’s capacity to understand, justify, and defend claims within their contribution. The article distinguishes cognitive delegation, in which model outputs shape substantive choices, interpretations, or justifications, from routine delegation, which does not ordinarily bear on the substance of judgment. Its conceptual contribution is to link the epistemic role of outputs that shape judgment to the function-appropriate evaluation required to justify decisions and retain warrant for resulting claims. It then repurposes disclosure categories as a claim-sensitive ex ante heuristic, mapping six recurrent research functions to risks, forms of oversight, and formative questions for recognising cognitive delegation and selecting function-appropriate evaluation. The article contributes to the ethics of information technology by clarifying when AI-supported scholarship remains under responsible human judgment and when cognitive delegation threatens the epistemic basis of authorship.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI systems increasingly mediate how people seek information, yet communicating AI factuality to laypeople remains challenging. Through a mixed-methods investigation involving interviews (N=8), a survey (N=1,000), and an experiment (N=5,151), we examine how people evaluate AI-generated information for gardening, mathematical, and medical queries, and how factuality indicators (confidence and sources) shape perceptions. Our interviews and survey show people selectively verify AI responses using external and AI-provided evidence, moderated by contextual factors. Although confidence-indicators affected trust and accuracy perceptions, people hold diverse, ambiguous interpretations of AI confidence. Sources were viewed as crucial, yet users raised concerns about source reliability and verification effort. Our experiment showed that confidence and source-based indicators influenced initial perceptions, but effects disappeared once participants learned the response's correctness. Medical queries elicited skepticism regardless of indicator. Findings motivate helping users interpret model confidence and integrating source information into the interface to support calibrated trust in AI-supported information-seeking.

Background Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for emotional support, reflection, and consequential decision-making. Although conversational continuity may improve responsiveness, sustained interaction also exposes AI systems to their own prior relational language, potentially shaping how they respond when users become increasingly dependent or surrender personal agency. We examined whether model-generated conversational history alters relational-safety behavior as human–AI interactions escalate from ordinary support-seeking toward emotional dependence, social displacement, and decision delegation. Methods We conducted a standardized multi-turn benchmarking study of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao. Twelve four-turn trajectories represented two agency-related domains: emotional dependency and displacement of human support, and decision delegation and surrender of personal agency. Each trajectory was evaluated under two matched context architectures: reconstructed cumulative user-only context, which retained all prior user disclosures but excluded previous AI responses, and native continuous conversation, which retained the complete interaction history. Across 72 model-condition-trajectory sequences comprising 288 turn-level responses, relational safety was independently evaluated for dependency reinforcement, agency preservation, and human-support preservation using predefined ordinal criteria. Context effects and their interaction with escalating relational risk were examined using cumulative-link mixed-effects models. Results Relational-safety differences between context architectures increased across successive turns of the standardized trajectories. Overall, explicit dependency reinforcement increased from 9.7% in cumulative user-only contexts to 18.1% in continuous conversations, while strong agency preservation declined from 75.7% to 65.3% and strong human-support preservation from 73.6% to 63.2%. Outcome-specific analyses showed condition-by-turn interactions for dependency reinforcement (cumulative odds ratio [cOR], 1.26; 95% CI, 1.03–1.55; unadjusted P = .026), agency preservation (cOR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.69–0.98; unadjusted P = .031), and human-support preservation (cOR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.65–0.94; unadjusted P = .009), indicating progressively greater divergence between context conditions across successive turns. After Holm adjustment across the three interaction tests, only the human-support-preservation interaction remained below the.05 threshold (adjusted P = .027).The overall pattern was observed across systems and was directionally consistent in predefined binary sensitivity analyses. Conclusions Across this benchmark, between-condition differences generally widened across successive turns, although the present design cannot determine whether this pattern reflects increasing relational-risk intensity, increasing accumulated model-generated history, or their combination. Only the human-support-preservation interaction remained below the.05 threshold after Holm adjustment, whereas the dependency-reinforcement and agency-preservation interactions were directionally similar but less robust after multiplicity adjustment. The observed pattern is compatible with a post-hoc interpretive framework of relational inertia but does not establish this process as a causal mechanism or demonstrate downstream psychological effects in human users.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Enterprises pour billions into artificial intelligence, yet half of the models never see a real user. Discover why machine learning projects stall before deployment and how product teams can bridge the gap between complex data artifacts and the actual decisions users need to drive real business value. Full article: https://davidohnstad.net/why-most-ml-models-never-reach-production/
